# **Abstract** {#abstract}

Bakery businesses frequently experience food waste because production decisions rely on manual judgement and uncertain daily demand, while short product shelf lives make overproduction difficult to recover. This project proposes a Smart Bakery Food Waste Reduction System to support a single bakery in predicting next-day demand, planning feasible production and managing unavoidable surplus. The system covers user and access management, demand prediction, inventory and production recommendation, point-of-sale simulation, leftover donation and waste management, reporting, system administration, and alerts and notifications. A tailored Agile methodology is adopted to support iterative requirements analysis, prototyping, design, implementation and user evaluation. The mobile application is designed using Flutter, with a Node.js and Express TypeScript backend, a Python FastAPI machine-learning service and a Supabase PostgreSQL database. Random Forest Regression is selected as the primary prediction model, while Linear Regression provides a baseline for comparison. Historical sales, temporal patterns, weather and public-holiday information are used as prediction inputs, and a configurable cold-start heuristic is applied when insufficient historical records are available. Inventory-aware recommendations limit production to feasible quantities, while the simulated point-of-sale process records sales, lost sales and leftovers without representing them as real bakery transactions. The proposed design is evaluated through unit, integration, system, usability, performance, security, reliability and compatibility testing. Prediction quality is assessed using chronological holdout data and the MAE, RMSE, MAPE and R² metrics. The resulting design provides an integrated and traceable approach to reducing avoidable bakery overproduction while supporting operational decision-making, surplus donation and performance monitoring. Its principal limitations are its single-bakery scope, dependence on simulated sales and external contextual services, and the absence of integration with a real point-of-sale system.

Chapter 1

**Introduction**

# **1 Introduction** {#1-introduction}

The bakery industry faces significant challenges in balancing daily production with customer demand. Producing excessive quantities of bakery products results in food waste and unnecessary operational costs, while producing insufficient quantities leads to stock-outs, lost sales, and customer dissatisfaction. Many small and medium-sized bakeries still rely on experience, intuition, or historical observations when determining daily production quantities, making it difficult to respond accurately to changing customer demand.

This project proposes the development of a Smart Bakery Food Waste Reduction System, an intelligent decision support system designed for a single bakery. The system applies machine learning techniques to predict next-day demand based on historical sales data together with contextual factors such as weather conditions, day-of-week patterns, seasonal trends, and public holidays. Instead of relying solely on demand prediction, the system combines predicted demand with ingredient inventory and recipe requirements to generate feasible production recommendations that support daily bakery operations.

In addition to demand prediction and production recommendation, the system includes inventory management, Point-of-Sale (POS) simulation, leftover and donation management, reporting and dashboard visualization, alerts and notifications, and system administration. Prediction generation, production-decision confirmation, model retraining, and sales simulation are initiated manually by authorised users through the mobile application rather than by background scheduling. These modules work together to support production planning, inventory monitoring, operational decision-making, and continuous evaluation of bakery performance while reducing unnecessary food waste.

The scope of this project is limited to a single bakery operation. The proposed system focuses on assisting bakery managers in making more informed production decisions through intelligent demand forecasting, inventory-aware production planning, and responsible surplus management. It does not include online customer ordering, payment processing, delivery services, marketplace functionality, or multi-branch bakery management.

## **1.1 Project Objectives** {#1.1-project-objectives}

The primary objective of this project is to develop a **Smart Bakery Food Waste Reduction System** that assists bakery managers in reducing food waste through intelligent demand prediction, inventory-aware production planning, and structured leftover management. The proposed system aims to improve daily bakery decision-making by replacing manual estimation with data-driven forecasting and recommendation features. Instead of only recording sales and inventory information, the system functions as a decision support tool that helps the bakery determine suitable production quantities, monitor ingredient availability, evaluate production outcomes, and manage unavoidable surplus responsibly.

To achieve this overall objective, the project is divided into four specific objectives, each addressing an important part of the food waste reduction process within a single bakery environment.

### **Objective 1: Develop an Accurate Next-Day Demand Prediction Model**  {#objective-1:-develop-an-accurate-next-day-demand-prediction-model}

The first objective is to develop a machine learning-based demand prediction model that can forecast the next day’s demand for different bakery product categories. The prediction model uses historical sales data together with relevant contextual factors such as day of the week, seasonal patterns, weather conditions, and public holidays. These factors are considered because customer demand for bakery products may change depending on time, weather, and calendar-related events.

The model is designed to support bakery managers in estimating how many products should be prepared for the following day. By improving the accuracy of demand estimation, the system helps reduce unnecessary overproduction while lowering the risk of underproduction and missed sales opportunities. In addition, the system includes prediction confidence, model evaluation, and model retraining features to ensure that the prediction process can be monitored and improved over time.

### **Objective 2: Generate Inventory-Aware Production Recommendations**  {#objective-2:-generate-inventory-aware-production-recommendations}

The second objective is to generate practical production recommendations by combining predicted demand with the bakery’s available inventory and production constraints. While the demand prediction model estimates customer demand, the smart recommendation component determines whether the predicted quantity can be produced based on ingredient availability, recipe requirements, and maximum producible quantity.

This objective ensures that production recommendations are not only demand-based, but also operationally feasible. If the available ingredients are insufficient to meet the predicted demand, the system can recommend adjusted production quantities and indicate possible shortages. This helps bakery managers make better production decisions, reduce ingredient wastage, and avoid unrealistic production plans.

### **Objective 3: Develop a POS Simulation Framework for System Testing and Validation**  {#objective-3:-develop-a-pos-simulation-framework-for-system-testing-and-validation}

The third objective is to develop a Point-of-Sale (POS) simulation framework to simulate daily bakery sales transactions for testing and validation purposes. Since the project may not have continuous access to real customer transaction data during development, the simulation framework provides a controlled method to generate realistic sales data and evaluate the system’s performance under different demand conditions.

The POS simulation uses relevant factors such as predicted demand, weather conditions, and calendar information to produce more realistic sales patterns. The generated results allow the system to compare production quantities, sold quantities, leftovers, and potential lost sales. This helps validate whether the demand prediction and production recommendation features can support better bakery planning before the system is applied in a real operational environment.

### **Objective 4: Implement Leftover and Donation Management**  {#objective-4:-implement-leftover-and-donation-management}

The fourth objective is to implement a leftover and donation management module to handle surplus bakery products at the end of the business day. Although accurate prediction and production planning can reduce food waste, it is difficult to completely eliminate leftovers because customer demand may still fluctuate unexpectedly.

Therefore, the system records leftover quantities by comparing produced quantities with sold quantities. Safe and edible surplus products can then be tracked for donation to charity partners. This objective supports responsible surplus management by reducing unnecessary disposal and improving transparency in donation activities. It also allows the bakery to monitor waste rates and evaluate the effectiveness of its food waste reduction efforts over time.

## **1.2 Project Background** {#1.2-project-background}

Food waste is a major issue in food retail and production. The bakery sector is particularly affected because many products, including bread, buns, cakes, and pastries, have a short shelf life and are expected to be sold while fresh (Goryńska-Goldmann et al., 2020; Goryńska-Goldmann et al., 2021; Mesiranta et al., 2025). When bakeries produce more items than customers actually purchase, the unsold products may become stale, lose their quality, or become unsuitable for sale. This results in financial loss for the bakery and contributes to unnecessary food waste.

For small and medium-sized bakeries, deciding the correct production quantity each day is a challenging task. Many bakeries still rely on the owner’s experience, staff estimation, or previous sales patterns when planning daily production. Although this manual approach may be useful in some situations, it is often not accurate enough to respond to changes in customer demand. Demand may increase or decrease due to weekdays, weekends, holidays, weather conditions, seasonal patterns, and local events. If these factors are not properly considered, the bakery may produce too much and create leftovers, or produce too little and experience stock-outs.

Overproduction and underproduction both create operational problems. Overproduction causes excess bakery products to remain unsold at the end of the day, increasing food waste and ingredient cost. Underproduction causes lost sales opportunities and may reduce customer satisfaction when popular products are unavailable. Therefore, bakeries need a more systematic method to estimate customer demand and plan production quantities more accurately.

In addition to demand uncertainty, bakery production is also affected by inventory and recipe constraints. Even if customer demand can be predicted, the bakery must still ensure that sufficient ingredients are available to produce the recommended quantity. For example, a bakery may predict high demand for a certain bread category, but the actual production may be limited by the availability of flour, butter, eggs, or other ingredients. This shows that demand prediction alone is not enough. A practical bakery system should also consider inventory levels, recipe requirements, and production feasibility before recommending daily production quantities.

To address these problems, this project proposes the development of a **Smart Bakery Food Waste Reduction System** for a single bakery operation. The system uses historical sales data and contextual information such as weather and calendar data to predict next-day demand for bakery product categories. The predicted demand is then combined with inventory and recipe information to generate feasible production recommendations. The system also includes manager-initiated POS simulation for testing, leftover tracking, donation management, reporting, alerts, and administrative functions to support daily bakery operations.

The scope of this project is limited to one bakery environment. This scope is suitable because the system can focus on localized sales patterns, bakery-specific product categories, and realistic operational constraints. The proposed system does not aim to function as an online ordering platform, marketplace system, or multi-branch enterprise system. Instead, it focuses on helping a bakery manager make better daily production decisions, reduce avoidable food waste, and manage unavoidable surplus in a more responsible and traceable manner.

## **1.3 Advantages & Contributions** {#1.3-advantages-&-contributions}

The Smart Bakery Food Waste Reduction System provides operational, environmental, and technical benefits that improve traditional bakery management. Instead of functioning only as a record-keeping application, the system acts as an intelligent decision support tool for small-scale bakeries. By integrating machine learning, inventory-aware production planning, and surplus management into daily bakery operations, the system helps bakery staff make better production decisions while reducing food waste. The proposed system benefits bakery operators, the local community, and demonstrates the practical application of intelligent software engineering in supporting sustainable food production. 

### **Advantage 1: Operational and Financial Efficiency** {#advantage-1:-operational-and-financial-efficiency}

The system improves bakery operations by reducing two common business problems which are overproduction and stock-outs. Using machine learning to predict customer demand enables the bakery to produce more accurate quantities each day, reducing the number of unsold products while maintaining sufficient stock during peak demand. This lowers ingredient costs, minimizes financial losses, and improves customer satisfaction by reducing missed sales opportunities. The integration of demand prediction with inventory monitoring also supports better ingredient purchasing decisions, ensuring sufficient raw materials are available without excessive inventory. These improvements enable bakeries to operate more efficiently while making better use of available food resources. 

### **Advantage 2: Contribution to Zero Hunger through Food Redistribution**  {#advantage-2:-contribution-to-zero-hunger-through-food-redistribution}

The system supports **Sustainable Development Goal 2 (Zero Hunger)** by reducing avoidable food waste and improving the utilization of edible bakery products. The primary contribution is the prevention of overproduction through intelligent demand prediction and inventory-aware production planning. By helping bakeries produce quantities that more closely match customer demand, the system reduces unnecessary surplus before food waste occurs. For surplus products that cannot be completely avoided, the system records and manages donation activities to local charity organizations or food banks. Instead of disposing of edible bakery products, the system supports responsible food redistribution to communities experiencing food insecurity. This dual approach of waste prevention and food redistribution maximizes food utilization while promoting sustainable bakery operations and social responsibility. 

### **Advantage 3: Technical Contribution to Intelligent Bakery Management**  {#advantage-3:-technical-contribution-to-intelligent-bakery-management}

From a technical perspective, this project demonstrates the practical integration of machine learning and software engineering within a small-scale bakery environment. Unlike conventional bakery management systems that mainly record operational data, the proposed system combines demand prediction, inventory-aware production recommendation, POS simulation, reporting, and leftover management into a single intelligent decision support platform. The project also demonstrates how data collected from daily bakery operations can be transformed into actionable recommendations that assist production planning and continuous operational improvement. By integrating predictive analytics with inventory management and surplus tracking, the proposed system provides a practical example of how intelligent software can support sustainable food production while remaining affordable and suitable for small and medium-sized bakeries. 

## **1.4 Project Scope** {#1.4-project-scope}

The project covers an Android-based decision-support system for one bakery. Its scope includes user access, demand prediction, ingredient and recipe management, FIFO inventory, production recommendations, manager-initiated sales simulation, leftover and donation management, dashboards, alerts, and administration. It excludes real POS hardware integration, customer ordering and payment, delivery and marketplace functions, multi-branch management, and automatic background scheduling. All major prediction, retraining, production-decision, and simulation actions are initiated by an authorised user.

### **1.4.2 System Functional Modules** {#1.4.2-system-functional-modules}

#### **Module 1: User and Access Management** {#module-1:-user-and-access-management}

This module manages user accounts and controls secure access to the system.  
**I. User Authentication**  
The system allows authorised users to securely log in and log out. It also manages active user sessions to ensure that protected system functions cannot be accessed without successful authentication.  
**II. Profile Management**  
Users can view and update their personal information, such as their name, contact information, and account details.  
**III. Access Control**  
The system restricts access to protected functions and business records. Users are only permitted to access functions and information associated with their assigned responsibilities.

#### **Module 2: Demand Prediction** {#module-2:-demand-prediction}

This is the core intelligent module of the system. It predicts the next day’s demand for each bread category using historical sales patterns, calendar-related information, weather conditions, and public holidays.  
**I. Historical Data Management**  
The system stores and manages historical sales and estimated-demand records. It also checks whether the available records are complete and suitable before they are used for prediction model training and evaluation.  
**II. Predictive Data Preparation**  
The system combines relevant information that may influence bakery demand. This includes previous sales, rolling averages, sales trends, same-weekday patterns, day of the week, weekends, months, monsoon seasons, weather conditions, public holidays, and selected events.  
**III. Manager-Initiated Demand Prediction**  
The manager can generate a next-day demand prediction for each bread category through the mobile application. The system uses the main prediction model and compares its performance with a simpler baseline model.  
**IV. Prediction Confidence Assessment**  
The system calculates a confidence level for each prediction. Predictions with low agreement or high uncertainty are highlighted so the manager can review them carefully before making a production decision.  
**V. Cold-Start Prediction**  
When fewer than 30 days of suitable historical data are available, the system generates predictions using predefined demand patterns and contextual adjustment factors. This allows the system to remain usable during its early operation.  
**VI. Model Training and Manual Retraining**  
The prediction model is trained using available historical data. An authorised user can initiate model retraining after sufficient new sales data have been collected.  
**VII. Model Evaluation**  
The system evaluates prediction performance using suitable accuracy measurements. It also compares the main prediction model with the baseline model to determine whether the selected model provides better results.  
**VIII. Prediction Explanation**  
The system displays the major factors that influenced each prediction, helping the manager understand why a particular demand quantity was generated.  
**IX. Model Version Management**  
The system stores model versions, training dates, data periods, and evaluation results. It also supports comparison between model versions and restoration of a previous valid model when necessary.

#### **Module 3: Inventory and Smart Production Recommendation** {#module-3:-inventory-and-smart-production-recommendation}

This module manages ingredients, bread categories, recipes, inventory batches, production feasibility, and production recommendations.  
**I. Ingredient Management**  
The administrator can add, view, update, and manage ingredient information, including ingredient name, measurement unit, reorder threshold, supplier information, and current available stock.  
**II. Bread Category Management**  
The administrator can manage bread category information, including category name, selling price, description, and active status.  
**III. Recipe Management**  
The administrator can define the ingredients required for each bread category and specify the quantity of each ingredient needed to produce one unit or batch.  
**IV. FIFO Inventory Management**  
The system records ingredient restocking as separate inventory batches. When ingredients are used, the system deducts stock from the oldest valid batch first and records every inventory movement for traceability.  
**V. Inventory Quality Validation**  
The system checks for expired ingredient batches, differences between recorded and calculated stock balances, and bread categories with incomplete or missing recipes.  
**VI. Low-Stock Detection**  
The system compares the available quantity of each ingredient with its reorder threshold. A low-stock event is generated when the available quantity falls below the required level.  
**VII. Production Feasibility and Constraint Checking**  
The system converts predicted bread demand into ingredient requirements and compares these requirements with available inventory. It calculates the maximum quantity that can be produced and identifies ingredients that limit production.  
**VIII. Smart Production Recommendation**  
The system combines predicted demand, recipe requirements, and available inventory to recommend a feasible production quantity for each bread category. When ingredients are insufficient, the system may suggest reduced production or ingredient restocking.  
**IX. Production Decision Management**  
The manager can accept, reduce, or override the recommended production quantity. The system records the final selected quantity and the reason provided when the manager changes the recommendation.

#### **Module 4: POS and Sales Simulation** {#module-4:-pos-and-sales-simulation}

This module simulates customer demand and bakery sales for system testing, prediction model learning, and production-strategy evaluation.  
**I. Production Decision Retrieval**  
The system retrieves the production quantities explicitly confirmed by the Bakery Manager for the selected simulation date. If the manager accepts a recommendation without adjustment, the recommended quantity is stored as the confirmed production quantity. The simulation cannot proceed without a confirmed production decision.   
**II. Manager-Initiated Sales Simulation**  
The manager can manually start the sales simulation through the mobile application. The simulation does not run automatically in the background.  
**III. Context-Aware Sales Simulation**  
The system simulates customer demand and purchase transactions using weather conditions, public holidays, time slots, and bread-category demand patterns.  
**IV. Stock-Limited Sales Processing**  
The system prevents simulated sales from exceeding the available quantity of bread. When simulated demand is higher than the available quantity, the unmet quantity is recorded as lost sales.  
**V. Sales Transaction Recording**  
The system records the bread category, quantity sold, unit price, transaction time, and subtotal for every simulated sales transaction. These records are used for reporting and prediction model training.  
**VI. Financial Snapshot Recording**  
The system records the selling price used during each transaction and estimates ingredient costs from recipe requirements and inventory batch costs. It then calculates simulated revenue and estimated gross profit.  
**VII. End-of-Day Result Aggregation**  
After the simulation is completed, the system summarizes production quantity, units sold, lost sales, leftovers, revenue, ingredient cost, and estimated gross profit. Estimated demand is calculated as the number of units sold plus lost sales.

#### **Module 5: Leftover, Donation and Waste Management** {#module-5:-leftover,-donation-and-waste-management}

This module manages unsold bakery products and records whether they are donated or discarded.  
**I. Leftover Calculation**  
The system automatically calculates the leftover quantity by subtracting the quantity sold from the quantity produced. Leftovers are recorded according to bread category and date.  
**II. Charity Partner Management**  
The administrator can manage charity partner information, including organization name, contact details, availability, and collection arrangements.  
**III. Donation Recommendation**  
The system identifies leftover products that are suitable for donation and suggests donation quantities based on product availability and shelf-life conditions.  
**IV. Donation Transaction Management**  
The system records donated bread categories, quantities, charity partners, transaction dates, and donation statuses such as pending, collected, completed, or cancelled.  
**V. Waste Recording**  
The system records leftover products that are discarded instead of donated. It stores the discarded quantity and the reason for disposal.  
**VI. Waste and Donation Performance Tracking**  
The system calculates leftover, donation, and waste rates. It also measures the quantity of bakery products diverted from disposal through donation.

#### **Module 6: Reporting and Dashboard** {#module-6:-reporting-and-dashboard}

This module presents prediction, inventory, sales, waste, donation, and estimated financial information to bakery users.  
**I. Prediction Dashboard**  
The dashboard displays predicted demand, prediction confidence, model accuracy, and important demand factors for each bread category. It also compares predicted demand with estimated actual demand.  
**II. Inventory Dashboard**  
The dashboard displays current ingredient quantities, low-stock ingredients, expiring inventory batches, inventory movements, and detected inventory-quality issues.  
**III. Sales Dashboard**  
The dashboard displays sales quantities, revenue trends, bread-category performance, time-slot sales distribution, and lost sales.  
**IV. Waste and Donation Dashboard**  
The dashboard displays leftover, donated, and discarded quantities. It also presents leftover, donation, and waste rates together with donation impact over time.  
**V. Financial Dashboard**  
The dashboard displays simulated sales revenue, estimated ingredient costs, and estimated gross profit. It may also compare waste levels with estimated gross profit to show the operational and financial impact of improved production planning.  
All financial values are clearly identified as simulation-based estimates and are used only for reporting. They do not influence demand predictions or production recommendations.  
**VI. Weekly Summary Report**  
The system generates a weekly summary of production, sales, prediction performance, inventory usage, lost sales, leftovers, donations, waste, and estimated financial performance.  
**VII. Report Export**  
Users can export selected reports in CSV and PDF format where the export function is implemented.

#### **Module 7: Alerts and Notifications** {#module-7:-alerts-and-notifications}

This module receives important events from other modules and presents them to authorised users without automatically executing prediction, production, retraining, or simulation processes.  
**I. Pending-Action Indicator**  
The system indicates whether the next-day prediction, production decision, or sales simulation has not yet been completed. The manager remains responsible for initiating each operation.  
**II. Ingredient Low-Stock Alert**  
The system notifies authorised users when an ingredient falls below its configured reorder threshold.  
**III. Expiring or Expired Ingredient Alert**  
The system notifies users when an ingredient batch is approaching its expiry date or has already expired.  
**IV. Low-Confidence Prediction Alert**  
The system alerts the manager when a generated prediction has a confidence level below the configured threshold.  
**V. Bread Stock-Out and Lost-Sales Alert**  
The system notifies the manager when simulated demand exceeds the selected production quantity and results in lost sales.  
**VI. Donation Status Notification**  
The system notifies relevant users when a donation is prepared, collected, completed, or cancelled.  
**VII. External Data Retrieval Alert**  
The system informs authorised users when required weather or holiday information cannot be retrieved, allowing them to retry the operation or continue using available data.  
**VIII. Notification Delivery**  
The system delivers in-application notifications while the application is active and background push notifications for event-based alerts when the application is not open.  
**IX. Notification Centre**  
The notification centre displays notification history and allows users to view and mark notifications as read. Where applicable, a notification links users to the related prediction, inventory, sales, or donation record.

#### **Module 8: System Administration** {#module-8:-system-administration}

This module manages bakery settings, system parameters, external-service configurations, audit records, and data protection functions.  
**I. Bakery Settings**  
The administrator can manage bakery information such as bakery name, operating hours, location type, simulation settings, and supported production-related settings.  
**II. System Parameter Management**  
The administrator can manage configurable values such as prediction-confidence thresholds, reorder levels, cold-start adjustment factors, shelf-life settings, and simulation parameters.  
**III. External Service Configuration**  
The system stores and manages the configuration required to retrieve weather and public holiday information and to deliver notifications. Sensitive configuration information is protected from normal users.  
**IV. System Logs and Audit Trail**  
The system records important user and system activities, including login activities, inventory changes, production decisions, prediction generation, manual retraining, simulation runs, configuration updates, and donation transactions.  
**V. Data Backup and Recovery Support**  
The system uses the available database backup and recovery mechanisms to protect operational and historical information from accidental loss and to support data restoration where necessary.

### **1.4.3 Non Functional** {#1.4.3-non-functional}

**1\. Performance**

The system shall generate demand predictions, production recommendations, dashboard information, and operational reports within an acceptable response time. Normal user operations, such as viewing inventory records, sales information, and notifications, should be completed without noticeable delay. This ensures that bakery staff can obtain updated information efficiently and make timely production and inventory decisions.

**2\. Security**

The system shall require users to authenticate before accessing its functions and data. Access to system features shall be controlled according to the user’s assigned role and permissions. Sensitive business information, including sales records, inventory data, prediction results, financial information, and system reports, shall be protected against unauthorised access, modification, and deletion. Secure authentication, database access policies, and protected communication shall be used to maintain data confidentiality and integrity.

**3\. Reliability**

The system shall operate consistently during normal daily bakery operations without frequent failures or interruptions. Important data, including sales transactions, inventory movements, production decisions, prediction results, donation records, and reports, shall be stored accurately and securely. The system shall also record failed user-initiated operations or external-service requests. Database backup and recovery mechanisms shall be used to reduce the risk of permanent data loss and support recovery after unexpected failures.

**4\. Usability**

The system shall provide a clear, consistent, and user-friendly interface that allows bakery staff to perform common tasks with minimal training. Navigation, form inputs, dashboard information, alerts, and error messages shall be presented clearly to reduce user mistakes and improve daily operational efficiency.

# **2 Literature Review** {#2-literature-review}

## **2.1 Introduction** {#2.1-introduction}

Bakery food waste is closely associated with short product shelf life, uncertain demand, overproduction, inventory limitations, and the absence of integrated decision support. The proposed Smart Bakery Food Waste Reduction System addresses these issues by combining machine-learning demand forecasting with inventory-aware production recommendations, manager-initiated sales simulation, leftover and donation management, reporting, and alerts. 

The purpose of this literature review is to evaluate research and software approaches that may support the proposed project, compare their strengths and limitations. Rather than discussing publications independently, the review is organized thematically. Section 2.2 examines bakery food-waste causes, prevention, and surplus recovery. Section 2.3 compares demand-forecasting models and contextual features. Sections 2.4 to 2.9 review development methodologies, requirements elicitation, design strategies, software architectures, testing methods, and enabling technologies. Section 2.10 compares related bakery forecasting and production-planning works. The chapter concludes by synthesizing the major findings.

## **2.2 Food Waste Reduction in Bakery Operations** {#2.2-food-waste-reduction-in-bakery-operations}

Food waste reduction in bakery operations has become an important research area because bakery products are highly perishable and often have a short shelf life. Bread and fresh pastry products must usually be sold within a limited period, making bakeries vulnerable to overproduction, unsold stock, and product returns. Existing studies show that bakery food waste is not caused by a single factor, but occurs across different stages of operation, including raw material storage, production, finished product handling, transportation, retail ordering, and surplus management.

### **2.2.1 Causes of Food Waste in Bakery Operations**  {#2.2.1-causes-of-food-waste-in-bakery-operations}

Several studies have investigated the causes of food losses in the baking and confectionery industry. Food losses occur across multiple bakery departments, including raw material storage, production, final product storage, and transport [(Goryńska-Goldmann et al., 2020\)](https://doi.org/10.3390/agriculture11010019). Their study showed that the production section generated the highest level of losses, while transport-related losses were mainly caused by errors in placed orders. This finding suggests that food waste in bakeries is not only caused by physical damage or spoilage, but also by planning and coordination problems. 

Similarly, bakery losses are influenced by technical, organizational, and human factors [(Goryńska-Goldmann et al., 2021\)](https://doi.org/10.3390/agriculture11100936). Their study identified dough forming and baking as high-risk stages because human errors, incorrect recipe handling, and deviations from production parameters can lead to product defects. The study also highlighted that smaller bakeries may experience lower food losses because their production is more closely matched to local demand. This finding is important for the proposed project because it shows that accurate demand estimation is strongly related to food waste reduction. 

Both studies agree that bakery food waste can occur throughout the operational process. However, their focus is mainly on identifying causes and recommending operational improvements such as staff training, equipment maintenance, process monitoring, and better inventory control. Although these strategies are useful, they rely heavily on manual management and staff experience. They do not provide an intelligent software-based approach to predict demand or recommend production quantities before production begins.

### **2.2.2 Operational Strategies for Reducing Bakery Food Waste** {#2.2.2-operational-strategies-for-reducing-bakery-food-waste}

Existing research also emphasizes the importance of operational improvements in reducing bakery food waste. Several prevention strategies were proposed including better employee training, improved production control, proper handling of raw materials, and reduction of ordering errors [(Goryńska-Goldmann et al., 2020\)](https://doi.org/10.3390/agriculture11010019). These recommendations are practical because they target the operational causes of food losses in bakeries.

This view was supported by identifying inventory management, process monitoring, and retailer cooperation as important strategies for reducing food losses [(Goryńska-Goldmann et al., 2021\)](https://doi.org/10.3390/agriculture11100936). The study found that FIFO inventory management, minimal stock levels, automated ingredient handling, and improved communication with retailers can help reduce raw material spoilage and finished product surplus. These findings show that food waste reduction requires not only better production practices, but also better planning and coordination between inventory, production, and sales activities. 

Discussion was extended by focusing on proactive operational planning in retail stores [(Riesenegger & Hübner, 2022\)](https://doi.org/10.3390/su14052494). Their study found that comprehensive databases, demand forecasting, weather information, assortment planning, and AI-assisted ordering can help reduce overstock of ultra-fresh products. Although the study focuses on grocery retail rather than bakery production, its findings are highly relevant because bakery products also face similar problems of freshness, overstock, and uncertain demand. The study supports the idea that information systems and intelligent decision support can improve food waste prevention.

These studies indicate that operational strategies are moving from reactive waste handling toward proactive planning. However, many existing approaches still do not fully integrate demand prediction, inventory constraints, and production recommendation into one bakery-specific system. These findings support integrating demand forecasting with inventory-aware production planning. 

### **2.2.3 Bread Surplus Management and Recovery Approaches** {#2.2.3-bread-surplus-management-and-recovery-approaches}

Besides preventing losses during production, some studies focus on managing surplus bread after it has already been produced. Bread surplus and waste were examined at the bakery-retail interface in Finland, Italy, and Sweden [(Mesiranta et al., 2025\)](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.clwas.2025.100433). Their study found that large product assortments, weak data sharing, ordering practices, and consumer expectations contribute to bread surplus. The study also reported that surplus bread is commonly managed through donations, discounted sales, breadcrumbs, brewing, recycling, and other recovery methods.

This study is valuable because it highlights the importance of collaboration between bakeries and retailers. Better information sharing and local demand data can help improve ordering accuracy and reduce surplus. It also shows that different countries and bakery systems use different recovery methods depending on their infrastructure, regulations, and food aid networks.

However, many of the solutions discussed by Mesiranta et al. are recovery-based rather than prevention-based [(Mesiranta et al., 2025\)](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.clwas.2025.100433). Donation, discounted sales, and upcycling can reduce disposal, but they are applied after surplus bread already exists. These methods are useful for managing unavoidable leftovers, but they do not directly address the root cause of overproduction. In contrast, the proposed system aims to reduce surplus before production by using demand forecasting and inventory-aware production recommendations, while still supporting leftover donation when surplus cannot be fully avoided.

### **2.2.4 Comparison of Existing Food Waste Reduction Approaches** {#2.2.4-comparison-of-existing-food-waste-reduction-approaches}

The reviewed literature presents several approaches for reducing bakery food waste. These approaches differ according to whether they prevent waste before production, control losses during operations, or manage surplus after production. Table 2.1 compares the main approaches according to their operational stage, focus, strengths, limitations, and suitability for the proposed system.

*Table 2.1: Comparison of Bakery Food Waste Reduction Approaches* 

| Approach | Supporting sources | Operational stage | Main focus | Strengths | Limitations |
| :---- | :---- | :---- | :---- | :---- | :---- |
| Employee training and process control | [(Goryńska-Goldmann et al., 2020\)](https://doi.org/10.3390/agriculture11010019), [(Goryńska-Goldmann et al., 2021\)](https://doi.org/10.3390/agriculture11100936) | During production | Improve recipe handling, equipment use, production monitoring, raw-material handling, and employee practices | Can reduce production errors, defective products, and avoidable losses without requiring complex technology | Effectiveness depends on employee knowledge, consistency, experience, and compliance with procedures |
| Inventory control and operational coordination | [(Goryńska-Goldmann et al., 2020\)](https://doi.org/10.3390/agriculture11010019), [(Goryńska-Goldmann et al., 2021\)](https://doi.org/10.3390/agriculture11100936) | Before and during production | Apply FIFO, maintain appropriate stock levels, improve ordering, and coordinate information between bakeries and retailers | Reduces ingredient spoilage, ordering errors, excessive inventory, and shortages | Primarily improves material management and may not prevent overproduction caused by inaccurate demand estimation |
| Demand forecasting and AI-assisted planning | [(Riesenegger & Hübner, 2022\)](https://doi.org/10.3390/su14052494) | Before ordering and production | Use historical data, weather information, comprehensive databases, forecasting, and AI-assisted ordering | Supports proactive decisions and can reduce overstock before waste occurs | Requires sufficient and reliable data; forecast errors may still result in overproduction or stock-outs |
| Donation, discounting, and surplus recovery | [(Mesiranta et al., 2025\)](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.clwas.2025.100433) | After production | Redistribute or recover unsold bread through donation, discounted sales, breadcrumbs, brewing, recycling, or upcycling | Prevents unavoidable surplus from being discarded and supports social or environmental benefits | Reactive because it manages surplus after overproduction has already occurred; additional coordination may be required |

The comparison shows that bakery food-waste reduction can involve both preventive and recovery-based approaches. Employee training and process control reduce losses caused by human and production errors, while inventory control reduces spoilage and ordering mistakes. However, these approaches do not directly determine how much bread should be produced according to expected customer demand.

Demand forecasting and AI-assisted planning provide a more proactive approach because production and ordering decisions can be adjusted before bakery products are produced. This approach is particularly relevant to products with short shelf lives because inaccurate production quantities can quickly become unsold waste. Nevertheless, forecasting cannot eliminate every source of surplus because unexpected changes in customer demand may still occur.

Donation, discounting, and other recovery methods remain useful for managing unavoidable leftovers. However, these methods should complement preventive planning rather than serve as the primary food-waste reduction approach.

Therefore, the proposed Smart Bakery Food Waste Reduction System primarily adopts **demand forecasting and inventory-aware production planning** to prevent overproduction. It also supports **inventory control** to improve ingredient usage and **donation recording** to manage unavoidable leftovers. Employee training and physical production-process control are not directly managed by the proposed software because they concern staff practices and bakery equipment operations.

## **2.3 Machine Learning for Demand Forecasting** {#2.3-machine-learning-for-demand-forecasting}

Demand forecasting plays an important role in production planning because inaccurate estimates can lead to overproduction, stock-outs, unnecessary inventory costs, and food waste. In bakery operations, forecasting is particularly important because many products have a short shelf life and must be produced before actual customer demand is known. Machine learning techniques provide an opportunity to improve demand estimation by identifying patterns from historical sales and contextual information such as weather, holidays, promotions, and seasonal trends.

Existing studies have evaluated a variety of statistical, machine learning, and deep learning approaches for sales forecasting. These include Linear Regression, Random Forest, XGBoost, Autoregressive Integrated Moving Average, Long Short-Term Memory, and Gated Recurrent Unit models. The reviewed studies show that model suitability depends on forecasting accuracy, dataset size, computational complexity, interpretability, and the ability to capture nonlinear demand patterns.

### **2.3.1 Random Forest for Sales and Demand Forecasting**  {#2.3.1-random-forest-for-sales-and-demand-forecasting}

Random Forest is an ensemble machine learning algorithm that combines predictions from multiple decision trees. Its ability to capture nonlinear relationships and interactions among multiple variables makes it suitable for sales forecasting problems where demand may be affected by historical, temporal, and external factors.

Random Forest Regression was evaluated using Walmart weekly sales data [(Kaveh Faraji Googerdchi & Jafari, 2025\)](https://doi.org/10.1109/iccit63348.2025.10989314). The model was trained with 100 decision trees and supported by data preprocessing and Recursive Feature Elimination to identify influential forecasting variables. The Random Forest model achieved an R² score of 0.9741 and significantly outperformed a naive baseline across MAE, RMSE, and MSE. Residual analysis also indicated that the model did not consistently overestimate or underestimate sales.

The study demonstrates that Random Forest can provide highly accurate forecasts for retail datasets and can identify important features that influence sales performance. Its use of multiple evaluation metrics and residual analysis strengthens the reliability of the findings. However, the model experienced reduced performance during extreme sales increases and decreases. It was also compared only with a simple naive baseline rather than stronger machine learning models.

Random Forest achieved strong forecasting performance when compared with Linear Regression, ARIMA, LSTM, and XGBoost [(Mustapha & Sithole, 2025\)](https://doi.org/10.47672/ajsas.2679). The Random Forest model obtained an R² value of approximately 0.9896, showing that it could explain most of the variance in the retail sales data. Although XGBoost and LSTM achieved slightly better results in that study, Random Forest remained a competitive model with lower implementation complexity than deep learning approaches.

Together, these studies indicate that Random Forest is effective for demand forecasting because it can model nonlinear relationships, work with multiple features, and achieve strong predictive performance. However, its performance depends on feature quality, hyperparameter selection, and the characteristics of the dataset.

### **2.3.2 Alternative Forecasting Models** {#2.3.2-alternative-forecasting-models}

Several studies emphasize that no single forecasting model performs best under every condition. Five forecasting methods were compared using five years of retail sales data from 50 products across 10 stores [(Mustapha & Sithole, 2025\)](https://doi.org/10.47672/ajsas.2679). The models included Random Forest, Linear Regression, ARIMA, LSTM, and XGBoost.

XGBoost achieved the lowest RMSE and the highest R² value, indicating the strongest overall forecasting performance. LSTM also achieved high accuracy but required greater computational resources and implementation complexity. Linear Regression provided competitive results despite its relatively simple assumptions, while ARIMA remained useful for modelling time-series patterns. Random Forest performed strongly but was not extensively optimized, which may have limited its final accuracy.

The findings illustrate the trade-off between prediction performance and practical implementation. XGBoost can achieve highly accurate results through gradient boosting and regularization, but it normally requires careful hyperparameter tuning. Deep learning models such as LSTM can capture complex temporal dependencies, but they generally require larger datasets, longer training time, and more computational resources. Random Forest offers a simpler and more maintainable alternative while still providing high forecasting accuracy.

A more advanced approach was explored by combining Random Forest and XGBoost in a hierarchical forecasting model for short-cycle agricultural products [(Li et al., 2024\)](https://doi.org/10.3390/foods13182936). Their method used a sliding time window, Grey Relational Analysis, Random Forest, residual clustering, and XGBoost. Random Forest first generated an initial forecast, while XGBoost learned additional patterns from the residual errors.

The hierarchical model achieved strong performance because it combined Random Forest’s robustness with XGBoost’s ability to refine prediction errors. It also demonstrated that relationships among different products could improve forecasting accuracy. However, the model required several preprocessing and modelling stages, increasing its computational and implementation complexity. Such an approach may be less practical for a small bakery with limited historical data and development resources.

Therefore, although advanced hybrid models may provide improved accuracy, a simpler forecasting model may be more suitable when maintainability, training time, available data, and system complexity are considered.

### **2.3.3 Linear Regression as a Baseline Model** {#2.3.3-linear-regression-as-a-baseline-model}

Linear Regression remains a commonly used forecasting method because it is simple, computationally efficient, and interpretable. The coefficients generated by the model allow users to understand how each independent variable affects the predicted outcome.

An application of Linear Regression to sales prediction showed that historical sales, promotions, marketing activities, weather, seasonal trends, and economic variables can support business forecasting [(Takale et al., 2022\)](https://doi.org/10.55529/jecnam.25.62.71). The study highlighted that Linear Regression provides a useful foundation for inventory planning, resource allocation, and strategic decision-making.

However, Linear Regression assumes that the relationship between input variables and sales is approximately linear. This assumption limits its ability to capture complex interactions among weather, holidays, seasonal patterns, and historical sales. It is also sensitive to outliers and multicollinearity and may underfit complicated demand patterns.

Despite these limitations, Linear Regression is suitable as a baseline because it provides a simple reference against which a more advanced model can be evaluated. In the proposed system, the Linear Regression model will be compared with Random Forest using MAE, RMSE, MAPE, and R². This comparison will determine whether the additional complexity of Random Forest produces meaningful improvements over a simple linear forecasting approach.

### **2.3.4 External and Contextual Features in Demand Forecasting**  {#2.3.4-external-and-contextual-features-in-demand-forecasting}

Forecasting accuracy depends not only on the selected algorithm but also on the quality and relevance of its input features. Demand is often influenced by external variables that cannot be represented using historical sales alone.

A weather-enhanced demand forecasting model was proposed using Rossmann retail sales data [(Ul Haq Qureshi et al., 2024\)](https://doi.org/10.1109/access.2024.3472499). The study integrated historical sales with weather conditions, store information, promotional activities, and other contextual variables. A GRU model with Grid Search optimization was then trained using weather-segmented data.

The findings showed that weather conditions significantly influence customer purchasing behaviour. Moderate weather was associated with stronger sales, while rain and snow reduced physical store visits and sales demand. The study also found that models trained using weather-specific subsets produced lower MAE and RMSE than models trained using a combined dataset.

This research supports the view that retail demand forecasting is a multivariate problem rather than a purely univariate time-series problem. Historical sales provide useful information, but external variables such as weather, holidays, store status, promotions, and seasonal conditions can improve forecasting performance.

Although the study used a GRU deep learning model, its findings are relevant to the proposed system because they justify the inclusion of contextual features. The Smart Bakery Food Waste Reduction System will therefore use historical sales together with day-of-week patterns, seasonal information, weather conditions, weekends, and public holidays when predicting next-day demand.

### **2.3.5 Comparison of Forecasting Models** {#2.3.5-comparison-of-forecasting-models}

The reviewed studies demonstrate that forecasting models differ in their ability to capture linear relationships, nonlinear interactions, temporal patterns, and contextual influences. They also differ in their data requirements, interpretability, computational complexity, and implementation effort. Table 2.2 compares the important forecasting models identified from the reviewed literature. 

Table 2.2: Comparison of Demand Forecasting Models

| Model | Supporting sources | Main strengths | Main limitations | Implementation complexity | Suitability for the proposed project |
| :---- | :---- | :---- | :---- | :---- | :---- |
| Linear Regression | [(Takale et al., 2022\)](https://doi.org/10.55529/jecnam.25.62.71),  [(Mustapha & Sithole, 2025\)](https://doi.org/10.47672/ajsas.2679) | Simple, fast, interpretable, and able to show how individual variables influence predicted demand | Assumes approximately linear relationships and may underfit complex interactions among sales, weather, holidays, and seasonal factors | Low | Suitable as a baseline model for determining whether a more advanced model provides meaningful improvement |
| ARIMA | [(Mustapha & Sithole, 2025\)](https://doi.org/10.47672/ajsas.2679) | Effective for modelling trends, seasonality, and time-dependent patterns in historical data | Requires appropriate time-series assumptions and is less flexible when handling numerous external and nonlinear variables | Moderate | Less suitable because the proposed system uses multiple historical, temporal, weather, and holiday-related features |
| Random Forest | [(Kaveh Faraji Googerdchi & Jafari, 2025\)](https://doi.org/10.1109/iccit63348.2025.10989314),  [(Mustapha & Sithole, 2025\)](https://doi.org/10.47672/ajsas.2679) | Captures nonlinear relationships, handles multiple features, is relatively resistant to overfitting, and provides feature-importance information | Does not model temporal sequences directly and may perform less effectively during extreme demand increases or decreases | Moderate | Highly suitable because it balances accuracy, flexibility, maintainability, and implementation effort |
| XGBoost | [(Mustapha & Sithole, 2025\)](https://doi.org/10.47672/ajsas.2679), [(Li et al., 2024\)](https://doi.org/10.3390/foods13182936) | Can achieve high prediction accuracy and progressively correct errors made by earlier decision trees | Requires careful hyperparameter tuning and may overfit if model settings are not properly controlled | Moderate to high | Potentially suitable, but its additional tuning requirements increase development and maintenance effort |
| LSTM and GRU | [(Mustapha & Sithole, 2025\)](https://doi.org/10.47672/ajsas.2679), [(Ul Haq Qureshi et al., 2024\)](https://doi.org/10.1109/access.2024.3472499) | Capture complex temporal dependencies and can process historical and contextual variables | Generally require larger datasets, longer training time, more computational resources, and more difficult model interpretation | High | Less suitable during the early project stage because the available bakery dataset may be limited |
| Hierarchical RF–XGBoost | [(Li et al., 2024\)](https://doi.org/10.3390/foods13182936) | Combines Random Forest robustness with XGBoost error correction and can use relationships among product categories | Requires several preprocessing, clustering, forecasting, and residual-correction stages | Very high | Not suitable for the current project because its complexity exceeds the requirements and resources of a single-bakery FYP |

The comparison shows that models with higher predictive capability frequently require greater data volume, computational resources, tuning effort, and implementation complexity. LSTM and GRU can capture complex temporal dependencies, while XGBoost and hierarchical models can achieve strong prediction accuracy. However, these models may be unnecessarily complex for a single-bakery system with limited historical data.

Linear Regression provides the lowest implementation complexity and the clearest interpretation. However, its linear assumptions may prevent it from capturing complex interactions among historical sales, weather, holidays, weekdays, and seasonal patterns. It is therefore more appropriate as a baseline than as the main prediction model.

Random Forest provides a stronger balance among forecasting accuracy, nonlinear modelling capability, implementation complexity, and maintainability. Unlike Linear Regression, it can capture complex interactions among multiple predictive variables. Compared with deep-learning and hybrid models, it requires less training data and implementation effort. Its feature-importance capability can also help explain which variables contribute to the demand predictions.

### **2.3.6 Model Selection for the Proposed System**  {#2.3.6-model-selection-for-the-proposed-system}

Based on the comparison, **Random Forest Regression** is selected as the main demand-prediction model for the Smart Bakery Food Waste Reduction System. It can process historical sales, temporal information, weather conditions, holidays, and other contextual variables while capturing nonlinear relationships among these features.

**Linear Regression** is selected as the baseline model because it is simple, interpretable, and computationally efficient. Comparing Random Forest with Linear Regression will determine whether the additional complexity of Random Forest produces a meaningful improvement in prediction accuracy.

The two models will be evaluated using MAE, RMSE, MAPE, and R². Random Forest will only be treated as the preferred model if its evaluation results demonstrate stronger and sufficiently reliable performance than the Linear Regression baseline.

## **2.4 Development Methodologies** {#2.4-development-methodologies}

The selection of an appropriate development methodology influences project planning, requirement management, testing, stakeholder feedback, and the ability to respond to changes. The proposed Smart Bakery Food Waste Reduction System consists of multiple modules and includes machine learning experimentation, external service integration, and interface development. Therefore, the selected methodology should provide sufficient structure while allowing iterative improvement.

### **2.4.1 Comparison of Agile, Waterfall, and Hybrid Approaches**  {#2.4.1-comparison-of-agile,-waterfall,-and-hybrid-approaches}

Waterfall emphasizes detailed upfront planning, stable requirements, sequential development stages, and a fixed project scope. It is suitable for projects whose requirements can be clearly defined at the beginning [(Thesing et al., 2021\)](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.procs.2021.01.227). Its structured planning improves predictability and documentation. However, incomplete or misunderstood early requirements may lead to costly changes during later development stages.

Agile supports short development cycles, regular feedback, continuous testing, and the refinement of requirements throughout development. This flexibility is useful when technical findings or stakeholder feedback may affect implementation decisions. An analysis of approximately 1,002 projects from more than 60 countries found a positive relationship between Agile practices and project success, stakeholder satisfaction, and efficiency [(Serrador & Pinto, 2015\)](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.ijproman.2015.01.006). The study also showed that Agile does not eliminate upfront planning but combines initial planning with continuous replanning during project execution. Nevertheless, Agile requires developer discipline, effective communication, and continuous requirement management.

Sitorus et al. found that Hybrid development combines Waterfall’s structured planning with Agile’s iterative implementation [(Sitorus et al., 2025\)](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.procs.2025.09.067). Their case study showed that Hybrid was most suitable when a project contained both stable and changing components. These findings indicate that methodology selection should depend on project characteristics rather than assuming that one approach is always superior.

### **2.4.2 Comparison of Development Methodologies** {#2.4.2-comparison-of-development-methodologies}

The reviewed literature shows that Waterfall, Agile, and Hybrid methodologies differ in their development process, requirement flexibility, stakeholder participation, testing practices, documentation, and project-management complexity. Table 2.3 compares these methodologies according to factors relevant to the proposed system.

*Table 2.3: Comparison of Software Development Methodologies*

| Comparison factor | Waterfall | Agile | Hybrid |
| :---- | :---- | :---- | :---- |
| Supporting sources | [(Thesing et al., 2021\)](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.procs.2021.01.227) | [(Sitorus et al., 2025\)](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.procs.2025.09.067),  [(Thesing et al., 2021\)](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.procs.2021.01.227), [(Serrador & Pinto, 2015\)](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.ijproman.2015.01.006) | [(Thesing et al., 2021\)](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.procs.2021.01.227),  [(Sitorus et al., 2025\)](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.procs.2025.09.067) |
| Development process | Development progresses sequentially through requirements, design, implementation, testing, and deployment | Development is divided into short, iterative increments that deliver and refine system functions | Uses structured planning from Waterfall together with iterative implementation from Agile |
| Requirement stability | Most requirements should be clearly defined and stable before development begins | Requirements can be refined or reprioritized during development | Stable requirements are planned initially, while uncertain requirements can be refined iteratively |
| Flexibility toward changes | Low because late requirement changes may affect completed phases and increase rework | High because changes can be incorporated into later iterations | Moderate to high, depending on which project activities follow Waterfall or Agile |
| Stakeholder feedback | Usually concentrated during requirement gathering and final acceptance | Obtained regularly throughout development | Obtained at selected stages and during iterative development activities |
| Testing approach | Testing is commonly performed after implementation has been substantially completed | Testing is performed continuously within development iterations | May combine phase-based testing with continuous testing during iterative development |
| Planning and documentation | Emphasizes detailed upfront planning and comprehensive documentation | Uses sufficient initial planning with continuous replanning and lightweight documentation | Maintains structured documentation while allowing adaptive planning |
| Main strengths | Predictable, structured, easy to manage, and suitable for stable requirements | Flexible, supports frequent feedback, detects problems earlier, and enables continuous improvement | Balances project control with flexibility for uncertain or changing components |
| Main limitations | Difficult to respond to late changes; misunderstood early requirements may cause expensive rework | Requires continuous planning, discipline, regular feedback, and active requirement management | More difficult to manage because the team must coordinate two development approaches |
| Suitability for the proposed project | Less suitable because interfaces, prediction features, and recommendation logic may require repeated refinement | Highly suitable because system modules and the prediction model can be developed, tested, and refined incrementally | Potentially suitable, but its additional process-management complexity is unnecessary for a single-developer FYP |

The comparison shows that Waterfall provides the greatest process structure and predictability when system requirements are stable. However, it is less suitable when technical findings or feedback may require changes after development has started. In the proposed project, the demand-prediction features, model parameters, production-recommendation rules, and mobile interfaces may require repeated testing and refinement. A strictly sequential process could therefore increase rework.

Hybrid development provides both structured planning and iterative implementation. This approach is useful when projects contain a combination of stable and changing components [(Sitorus et al., 2025\)](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.procs.2025.09.067). Nevertheless, Hybrid requires the developer to manage and coordinate two development approaches, which may introduce unnecessary process complexity for a single-developer academic project.

Agile provides the strongest flexibility for the proposed system. A positive relationship was found between Agile practices and project success, stakeholder satisfaction, and project efficiency [(Serrador & Pinto, 2015\)](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.ijproman.2015.01.006). Their findings also demonstrate that Agile does not eliminate initial planning; instead, it combines upfront planning with continuous replanning throughout development.

### **2.4.3 Suitability of the Development Methodology** {#2.4.3-suitability-of-the-development-methodology}

Based on the comparison, **Agile** is suitable as the development methodology for the Smart Bakery Food Waste Reduction System. The system consists of several modules that can be implemented and evaluated incrementally, including User and Access Management, Demand Prediction, Inventory and Smart Recommendation, POS Simulation, Leftover and Donation Management, Reporting and Dashboard, System Administration, and Alerts and Notifications.

Agile also supports the experimental nature of machine-learning development. The Random Forest model and Linear Regression baseline may require repeated feature refinement, training, evaluation, and parameter adjustment. Similarly, mobile interfaces and operational workflows can be improved after prototype evaluation and supervisor feedback.

Although Agile is suitable, the project will still maintain an initial project scope, documented requirements, architecture, schedule, and milestones. This does not make the project Hybrid because initial planning is also compatible with Agile development. The defining characteristic is that implementation, testing, feedback, and refinement will occur iteratively throughout the project.

## **2.5 Requirement Elicitation Methods**  {#2.5-requirement-elicitation-methods}

Requirement elicitation is conducted to identify and understand the functions, constraints, workflows, and quality expectations of a proposed system. Selecting appropriate elicitation techniques is important because each technique collects a different type of information and requires different levels of stakeholder participation, preparation, time, and cost. For the Smart Bakery Food Waste Reduction System, the elicitation techniques should support the understanding of bakery operations and allow the proposed mobile interfaces and system workflows to be evaluated before full implementation. 

### **2.5.1 Document Analysis**  {#2.5.1-document-analysis}

Document Analysis is an indirect elicitation technique that obtains requirements by examining available materials describing an organization, business process, existing system, or operational environment. The documents may include business records, reports, process descriptions, policies, existing system documentation, forms, data structures, and descriptions of comparable solutions.

Document Analysis supports the collection of background information and contextual understanding of a business need [(Huchenko & Gobov, 2020\)](https://doi.org/10.15439/2020f16). It can also be used to examine how existing solutions are implemented. Their survey involving 328 software project specialists found that Document Analysis was used by 87% of respondents, making it the second-most frequently applied elicitation technique after interviews. The study also found that Document Analysis was particularly common in outsourcing projects, where development teams needed to understand unfamiliar client systems and business environments.

Document Analysis is suitable for the proposed project because relevant requirements can be obtained by examining bakery food-waste studies, demand-forecasting literature, related bakery systems, sales and inventory data structures, recipe and ingredient information, existing bakery workflows, and project documentation. These materials can help identify the information required by functions such as demand prediction, production recommendation, inventory management, POS simulation, leftover management, donation recording, reporting, and notifications.

The technique requires less direct stakeholder involvement and provides traceable evidence for the identified requirements. However, its effectiveness depends on the availability, accuracy, completeness, and currency of the documents. Existing documents may describe current operations but may not reveal undocumented practices or users’ expectations for a new system. Therefore, Document Analysis should be complemented by a technique that allows the proposed solution to be visualized and validated.

### 

### **2.5.2 Prototyping** {#2.5.2-prototyping}

Prototyping involves creating an early representation of a proposed system so that its functions, interface design, navigation, and workflows can be examined before full implementation. A prototype may range from a paper sketch to a high-fidelity interactive interface.

A review of 140 studies concerning requirements elicitation techniques found that Prototyping can reduce requirement ambiguity by allowing stakeholders to visualize and validate a proposed solution [(Pacheco et al., 2018\)](https://doi.org/10.1049/iet-sen.2017.0144). Instead of relying entirely on verbal or written descriptions, stakeholders can examine how system functions may operate and identify missing, unclear, or unsuitable requirements.

Unstructured Interviews, Joint Application Development, and Paper Prototyping were compared through a family of experiments [(Rueda et al., 2020\)](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.infsof.2020.106361). Paper Prototyping identified the highest number of total and functional requirements and provided a strong balance between requirement quality and the time required to conduct the elicitation process. This indicates that Prototyping is particularly useful for identifying requirements concerning system interactions and interface behaviour.

Similarly, Prototyping was used by 67% of the surveyed software specialists [(Huchenko & Gobov, 2020\)](https://doi.org/10.15439/2020f16). They explained that it supports the elicitation and validation of stakeholder needs through an iterative model of the proposed solution. It can also improve users’ understanding of the system, evaluate alternative designs, and provide a basis for developing the final software.

For the proposed system, Prototyping can be used to represent mobile interfaces and workflows such as viewing demand predictions, initiating predictions, reviewing production recommendations, managing inventory, running the POS simulation, recording leftovers and donations, and viewing reports. Feedback on the prototypes can identify unclear navigation, missing information, unsuitable terminology, and incomplete workflows before substantial development effort is invested.

Nevertheless, a prototype may cause evaluators to focus mainly on interface appearance rather than underlying business rules and non-functional requirements. A prototype may also create unrealistic expectations if users assume that every displayed function has already been implemented. Therefore, the purpose and level of completion of each prototype should be clearly communicated.

### **2.5.3 Comparison of Requirement Elicitation Techniques**  {#2.5.3-comparison-of-requirement-elicitation-techniques}

The reviewed papers discuss different requirement elicitation techniques that vary in the type of information collected, required stakeholder involvement, time, strengths, and limitations. Table 2.4 compares five important techniques identified from the reviewed literature. The comparison is used to determine which techniques are most appropriate for the proposed Smart Bakery Food Waste Reduction System. 

*Table 2.4: Comparison of Requirement Elicitation Techniques*

| Technique | Findings from the reviewed papers | Main strengths | Main limitations | Suitability for the proposed project |
| :---- | :---- | :---- | :---- | :---- |
| Interviews | Interviews were the most frequently used technique, with a usage rate of 89% among the practitioners [(Huchenko & Gobov, 2020\)](https://doi.org/10.15439/2020f16). Unstructured interviews were found to require less preparation and could be conducted quickly [(Rueda et al., 2020\)](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.infsof.2020.106361). | Allow detailed explanations, immediate clarification, and follow-up questions about stakeholder needs | Depend heavily on the knowledge and availability of interviewees; responses may be subjective or incomplete | Less suitable because access to experienced bakery stakeholders is limited |
| Questionnaires | Questionnaires have been recognised as a technique for collecting standardised information from a large and potentially distributed group [(Pacheco et al., 2018](https://doi.org/10.1049/iet-sen.2017.0144); [Huchenko & Gobov, 2020\)](https://doi.org/10.15439/2020f16). | Can collect information from many respondents within a relatively short period and at low cost | Responses may be brief or unclear, and follow-up clarification is difficult; useful results require a sufficiently large and representative sample | Not suitable because the project does not have access to a large group of representative bakery users |
| Joint Application Development | JAD was found to be effective in identifying non-functional requirements through structured collaboration among participants [(Rueda et al., 2020\)](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.infsof.2020.106361). | Promotes discussion, requirement agreement, prioritization, and consideration of different stakeholder perspectives | Requires multiple stakeholders, extensive coordination, preparation, time, and skilled facilitation | Not suitable for a single-developer FYP with limited stakeholder participation |
| Document Analysis | Document Analysis was used by 87% of the practitioners [(Huchenko & Gobov, 2020\)](https://doi.org/10.15439/2020f16). The technique was particularly useful when development teams needed to understand unfamiliar existing systems and business environments | Provides traceable information about existing processes, business rules, data, problems, and system functions without requiring extensive stakeholder involvement | Available documents may be outdated, incomplete, inaccurate, or unable to reveal undocumented user expectations | Highly suitable because bakery studies, related systems, workflow descriptions, recipes, sales and inventory structures, and project documents can be examined |
| Prototyping | Prototyping was found to help users visualize and validate requirements [(Pacheco et al., 2018\)](https://doi.org/10.1049/iet-sen.2017.0144). Paper prototyping was found to identify the highest number of total and functional requirements [(Rueda et al., 2020\)](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.infsof.2020.106361). A usage rate of 67% was reported [(Huchenko & Gobov, 2020\)](https://doi.org/10.15439/2020f16) | Makes abstract requirements visible and helps identify missing functions, unclear navigation, unsuitable workflows, and usability issues | Requires time to create and revise; evaluators may focus on appearance while overlooking business rules and non-functional requirements | Highly suitable for evaluating the proposed mobile interfaces, demand-prediction presentation, production recommendations, inventory workflows, simulation, and reporting functions |

The comparison shows that Interviews, Questionnaires, and Joint Application Development depend heavily on access to suitable stakeholders. Interviews can obtain detailed explanations, but their effectiveness depends on the interviewee’s domain knowledge and availability. Questionnaires are more appropriate when requirements must be obtained from a large population, while JAD is suitable when several stakeholders can participate in structured collaborative sessions.
