These conditions do not match the limited stakeholder access and single-developer structure of the proposed project.

Document Analysis and Prototyping have different but complementary strengths. Document Analysis is suitable for building an initial understanding of bakery operations, food-waste problems, data requirements, business rules, and existing solutions. However, documents alone may not reveal how users expect to interact with the proposed application. Prototyping addresses this weakness by converting the initial requirements into visible interfaces and workflows that can be evaluated and refined.

### **2.5.4 Suitability of the Requirement Elicitation Techniques**  {#2.5.4-suitability-of-the-requirement-elicitation-techniques}

Based on the comparison, **Document Analysis and Prototyping** are suitable as the primary requirement elicitation techniques for the Smart Bakery Food Waste Reduction System.

Document Analysis will first be used to examine bakery food-waste literature, demand-forecasting studies, related bakery systems, workflow descriptions, recipe and inventory information, data structures, and existing project documents. This process will support the identification of the initial functional requirements, non-functional requirements, business rules, data requirements, and system constraints.

Prototyping will then be used to present the proposed mobile interfaces and workflows, including demand prediction, production recommendation, inventory management, POS simulation, leftover and donation recording, reporting, and notifications. Feedback obtained from prototype evaluation will be used to refine unclear, incomplete, or unsuitable requirements before full implementation.

Therefore, Document Analysis provides the initial domain and operational understanding, while Prototyping supports the visualization and validation of the proposed solution. Their complementary functions make them more appropriate for this project than Interviews, Questionnaires, or Joint Application Development. 

## **2.6 Design Strategies**  {#2.6-design-strategies}

Software design strategies influence how a system is divided, implemented, maintained, tested, and extended. An appropriate design strategy should reduce complexity, promote separation of responsibilities, and support future modification. The proposed Smart Bakery Food Waste Reduction System contains multiple functional modules, including demand prediction, inventory management, POS simulation, leftover and donation management, reporting, and notifications. Therefore, object-oriented, modular, and component-based design strategies are reviewed for their suitability. 

### **2.6.1 Object-Oriented Design**  {#2.6.1-object-oriented-design}

Object-oriented design organizes software around classes and objects that contain related data and behaviours. It supports principles such as encapsulation, abstraction, inheritance, and polymorphism, which can improve software maintainability, reusability, and extensibility.

Object-oriented design practices vary in importance and should be selected according to project characteristics [(Bräuer et al., 2017\)](https://doi.org/10.1109/seaa.2017.14). Their study evaluated 49 design practices and identified avoiding duplicate code, public fields, and package dependency cycles as important practices for improving software quality. Clear class responsibilities and controlled dependencies can also make software easier to understand and maintain.

The study provides practical guidance for improving object-oriented software design. However, it focuses primarily on Java-based systems and evaluates developers’ perceptions of design practices rather than measuring their effects on complete software projects. It also provides limited discussion of mobile applications, machine learning systems, and cloud-integrated software.

Object-oriented design remains relevant to the proposed system because Dart supports object-oriented programming through classes, objects, interfaces, encapsulation, and inheritance. The strategy can be used to represent entities such as users, bread categories, ingredients, inventory batches, sales records, prediction results, and notifications. However, object-oriented design alone does not explain how the entire system should be divided into major functional areas.

### **2.6.2 Modular Design**  {#2.6.2-modular-design}

Modular design divides a software system into separate functional modules, with each module responsible for a specific group of related operations. This reduces overall system complexity and allows modules to be developed, tested, maintained, and modified with fewer effects on other parts of the system.

An examination of modular design in ERP systems found that it improves flexibility and scalability by allowing organizations to implement and extend system functions incrementally [(Li et al., 2024\)](https://doi.org/10.54254/2755-2721/93/20240955). Independent modules can simplify maintenance and future enhancements because changes can be concentrated within the affected functional area.

Nevertheless, modular design can introduce integration challenges. Poorly defined module boundaries may lead to duplicated data, inconsistent information, incompatible interfaces, and complex dependencies. Standardised interfaces, centralized data repositories, and appropriate integration mechanisms are required to maintain consistent information exchange among modules [(Li et al., 2024\)](https://doi.org/10.54254/2755-2721/93/20240955).

Although the study focuses on large ERP systems, its findings are applicable to the proposed bakery system because both contain several integrated business functions. The proposed system can be divided into user management, demand prediction, inventory and recommendation, POS simulation, leftover and donation, reporting, administration, and notification modules. A shared database and clearly defined data structures can reduce inconsistency between these modules.

### **2.6.3 Component-Based Software Engineering** {#2.6.3-component-based-software-engineering}

Component-Based Software Engineering develops systems by assembling independent components that provide clearly defined functions through specified interfaces. Components can be developed and maintained separately, provided that their required and provided interfaces are compatible.

The importance of explicitly defining component interfaces and dependencies was highlighted [(Ning, 1997\)](https://doi.org/10.1109/AST.1997.599909). Clearly specified interfaces reduce direct dependency between components and make it easier to replace, extend, or reuse individual parts of a system. Component compatibility must also be verified to ensure that independently developed components can exchange information correctly.

A major advantage of CBSE is that it supports reuse, flexibility, and independent maintenance. However, component integration can become difficult when different components use incompatible interfaces, communication mechanisms, or data structures. The study also relies on older middleware technologies such as CORBA, which limits its direct applicability to modern mobile and cloud-based development. Nevertheless, its fundamental principles concerning component independence and interface specification remain relevant.

In the proposed system, functions such as authentication, prediction, weather retrieval, holiday retrieval, notification delivery, and database access can be treated as separate components or services. Each component should expose a clearly defined interface and avoid unnecessary dependency on the internal implementation of other components.

### **2.6.4 Comparison of Design Strategies**  {#2.6.4-comparison-of-design-strategies}

The reviewed design strategies organize software from different perspectives. Object-Oriented Design structures software around classes and objects, Modular Design divides the system according to functional responsibilities, while Component-Based Software Engineering constructs software using independent components with defined interfaces. Table 2.5 compares these strategies based on their structure, strengths, limitations, and suitability for the proposed system.

*Table 2.5: Comparison of Software Design Strategies*

| Comparison factor | Object-Oriented Design | Modular Design | Component-Based Software Engineering |
| :---- | :---- | :---- | :---- |
| Supporting source | [(Bräuer et al., 2017\)](https://doi.org/10.1109/seaa.2017.14) | [(Li et al., 2024\)](https://doi.org/10.54254/2755-2721/93/20240955) | [(Ning, 1997\)](https://doi.org/10.1109/AST.1997.599909) |
| Main design focus | Organizes data and behaviours into classes and objects | Divides a system into separate functional modules | Assembles independent and reusable software components through defined interfaces |
| Main design unit | Class or object | Functional module | Software component or service |
| Separation of responsibilities | Achieved through classes with clearly defined attributes and methods | Achieved by assigning each module a specific group of system functions | Achieved through independent components that expose required and provided interfaces |
| Main strengths | Supports encapsulation, abstraction, code reuse, maintainability, and extensibility | Reduces system complexity and allows modules to be developed, tested, and maintained separately | Supports component reuse, replacement, independent development, and integration with external services |
| Main limitations | Poor class design may produce excessive dependencies, duplicated code, or classes with unclear responsibilities | Poorly defined module boundaries may cause duplicated data, inconsistent information, and complex dependencies | Incompatible interfaces, data formats, or component versions may create integration and maintenance problems |
| Application in the proposed system | Represents entities such as users, bread categories, ingredients, inventory batches, sales, predictions, and donations as classes and objects | Separates the system into User Management, Demand Prediction, Inventory and Recommendation, POS Simulation, Leftover and Donation, Reporting, Administration, and Notification modules | Supports prediction services, weather and holiday APIs, database access, and notification services through defined interfaces |
| Overall suitability | Suitable for organizing the internal application code and domain entities | Highly suitable as the primary strategy because the system already consists of clearly defined functional modules | Suitable as a supporting strategy for integrating services and reusable components |

Object-Oriented Design is useful for organizing the internal code and domain entities of the proposed system. Its use of classes, objects, and encapsulation can improve maintainability and reduce unnecessary access to internal data. However, Object-Oriented Design alone does not define how the complete system should be divided into major functional areas.

Component-Based Software Engineering is useful for integrating independent services such as demand prediction, database access, weather information, holiday information, and notification delivery. Nevertheless, adopting it as the main design strategy may introduce unnecessary interface and integration complexity for a single-developer project.

Modular Design is the most suitable primary strategy because the proposed system already consists of well-defined functional modules. It enables each module to be implemented and tested separately before system integration. Clear module boundaries also reduce the effect of changes made to one functional area on other parts of the system.

### **2.6.5 Suitability of the Design Strategies** {#2.6.5-suitability-of-the-design-strategies}

Based on the comparison, the review indicates that the **Modular Design** is suitable as the primary design strategy for the Smart Bakery Food Waste Reduction System. The system will be divided into the following functional modules:

* User and Access Management  
* Demand Prediction  
* Inventory and Smart Recommendation  
* POS Simulation  
* Leftover and Donation Management  
* Reporting and Dashboard  
* System Administration  
* Alerts and Notifications

Each module will have a clearly defined responsibility and will communicate with other modules through controlled data structures and interfaces. This separation supports incremental Agile development, independent module testing, easier maintenance, and future system enhancement.

Object-Oriented Design will support the internal implementation of the modules by representing system entities and business logic using classes and objects. Component-based principles will support the integration of the prediction service, external APIs, database operations, and notification services. Therefore, these two strategies act as supporting design principles, while Modular Design remains the main selected strategy.

## **2.7 Software Architectures** {#2.7-software-architectures}

Software architecture defines the high-level structure of a software system and the interactions among its major components. Selecting an appropriate architecture is important because it influences maintainability, scalability, testability, security, and system integration. The proposed Smart Bakery Food Waste Reduction System consists of a Flutter mobile application, a TypeScript backend, a cloud database, a machine learning prediction component, and several external services. Therefore, layered architecture, Model View Controller architecture, and client-server architecture are reviewed.

### **2.7.1 Layered Architecture** {#2.7.1-layered-architecture}

Layered architecture separates software responsibilities into distinct layers, with each layer providing specific services to the layer above it. Common layers include the presentation layer, application or business logic layer, service layer, and data-access layer. This separation reduces direct dependencies and makes the system easier to understand, test, and maintain.

The study on layered architecture for smart mobile distributed systems proposed an architecture that distributes responsibilities between mobile devices and more capable server-side components [(Yesenia et al., 2025\)](https://doi.org/10.3390/app15073664). The architecture allowed lightweight interface operations to be performed on mobile devices while resource-intensive processing and data management were handled by servers. It also demonstrated that clearly defined layers can improve modularity, maintainability, extensibility, testing, security, and component reuse.

A major strength of the study is that the architecture was instantiated and evaluated in a practical emergency-management system rather than being discussed only theoretically. The evaluation considered both functional and non-functional requirements. However, the proposed architecture was designed for emergency systems, which require stricter availability, real-time communication, and disconnection handling than a bakery management application. It may therefore contain more distributed components and architectural complexity than required for a single-developer FYP.

Nevertheless, its separation of concerns principles are relevant to the proposed system. A simplified layered structure can separate the Flutter interface, controllers, business logic, repositories, data-access operations, prediction services, and external APIs.

### **2.7.2 Model View Controller Architecture** {#2.7.2-model-view-controller-architecture}

Model View Controller separates an application into three main elements. The Model represents system data and business entities, the View presents information to users, and the Controller processes user requests and coordinates interactions between the View and Model.

MVC is widely used in web, enterprise, and mobile applications because it supports separation of concerns [(Necula, 2024\)](https://doi.org/10.20944/preprints202404.1860.v1). By isolating user-interface logic from data and control logic, MVC can improve maintainability, code reuse, scalability, and testability. The study also noted that MVC remains relevant despite the development of related approaches such as MVVM and component-based frontend architectures.

MVC is suitable for data-intensive applications because changes to the user interface can be made without directly modifying the underlying data structures and business logic. Similarly, changes to request-processing logic can be implemented in controllers without redesigning every interface screen. This is useful for the proposed system, which contains interfaces for inventory management, demand prediction, sales simulation, reporting, donations, and notifications.

However, the reviewed study mainly provides a broad literature and bibliometric analysis rather than experimentally comparing MVC with alternatives such as MVVM or Clean Architecture. MVC may also lead to large or tightly coupled controllers if responsibilities are not properly separated.

In the proposed system, Flutter screens and widgets represent the View. The TypeScript backend implements the Controller and Model responsibilities. Controllers receive and validate requests from the Flutter application, while backend models represent entities. Services contain the main business logic, while repositories manage communication between the services and Supabase. This implementation extends the basic MVC structure with service and repository layers to improve separation of responsibilities and maintainability.

### **2.7.3 Client Server Architecture** {#2.7.3-client-server-architecture}

Client server architecture separates the system into clients that request services and servers that process requests, manage shared data, and provide centralized functionality. In mobile applications, the client commonly handles presentation and user interaction, while the server performs data processing, authentication, storage, and resource-intensive operations.

A review of mobile client-server computing found that responsibilities can be distributed differently depending on device capabilities and network conditions [(Jing et al., 1999\)](https://doi.org/10.1145/319806.319814). Thin-client systems transfer most application processing to the server, while thicker clients perform more processing locally. The study also highlighted the importance of synchronization, communication efficiency, cache management, and data consistency.

The architecture provides several advantages for the proposed system. Centralized storage allows multiple users or modules to access consistent bakery data, while prediction processing, and external API communication can be managed outside the mobile interface. It also enables the mobile application to remain relatively lightweight.

However, the study was published before modern cloud computing, REST APIs, smartphones, and Backend-as-a-Service platforms became widely adopted. Technologies such as broadcast disks, early mobile caching methods, and low-bandwidth wireless models are less relevant to current applications. Nevertheless, the fundamental principle of separating mobile clients from centralized services remains applicable.

For the proposed system, the Flutter application acts as the client, while the TypeScript backend, Supabase database, machine learning functions, and external APIs provide server-side services.

### **2.7.4 Comparison of Software Architectures**  {#2.7.4-comparison-of-software-architectures}

Layered Architecture, MVC, and Client–Server Architecture address different aspects of software organization. Layered Architecture separates internal responsibilities, MVC organizes interactions among the interface, request control, and data models, while Client–Server Architecture distributes processing and data management between client and server components. Table 2.6 compares their roles, strengths, limitations, and suitability for the proposed system. 

*Table 2.6: Comparison of Software Architectures* 

| Comparison factor | Layered Architecture | Model View Controller | Client-Server Architecture |
| :---- | :---- | :---- | :---- |
| Supporting source | [(Yesenia et al., 2025\)](https://doi.org/10.3390/app15073664) | [(Necula, 2024\)](https://doi.org/10.20944/preprints202404.1860.v1) | [(Jing et al., 1999\)](https://doi.org/10.1145/319806.319814) |
| Main focus | Separates system responsibilities into logical layers | Separates application data, user interfaces, and interaction control | Separates service-requesting clients from centralized servers |
| Main structure | Presentation, business logic, service, repository, and data-access layers | Model, View, and Controller | Mobile client, backend server, database, prediction service, and external services |
| Separation of responsibilities | Each layer performs a specific role and communicates through controlled boundaries | The Model manages data, the View displays information, and the Controller processes user actions | The client manages presentation and user interaction, while servers manage shared data and processing |
| Main strengths | Improves maintainability, testability, modularity, security, and separation of concerns | Separates interface code from data and control logic, supporting interface modification and testing | Provides centralized data management, shared services, server-side processing, and lightweight mobile clients |
| Main limitations | Additional layers may increase code volume and data-transfer complexity | Controllers may become large or tightly coupled if responsibilities are not properly controlled | Depends on network and server availability and may experience communication latency |
| Application in the proposed system | Separates Flutter interfaces, controllers, business logic, repositories, services, and data access | Uses Flutter screens and widgets as the View, while the TypeScript backend implements Controllers, Models, services, and repositories  | Connects the Flutter application with the backend, cloud database, prediction service, and external APIs |
| Overall suitability | Highly suitable for organizing internal system responsibilities  | Suitable as a supporting pattern within the Layered Client–Server Architecture for separating the Flutter View from backend request processing, business logic, and data models  | Highly suitable for distributing mobile and server-side responsibilities  |

Layered Architecture provides a clear internal separation of responsibilities. It allows presentation, request handling, business logic, prediction processing, external-service communication, and database access to be maintained and tested separately. However, excessive layering should be avoided because a small academic project does not require the complexity of a large enterprise architecture.

MVC supports the separation between the Flutter View and the TypeScript backend’s Controllers and Models. However, MVC alone does not fully explain how the complete system is distributed or how additional service and repository responsibilities should be organized. It is therefore incorporated as a supporting pattern within the broader Layered Client–Server Architecture.  

Client–Server Architecture defines the distribution between the Flutter mobile client and server-side components. However, it does not provide sufficient guidance for organizing the internal responsibilities of those components. Layered Architecture addresses this limitation by separating the controller, business logic, service, repository, and data-access responsibilities.

Therefore, these architectures are complementary rather than mutually exclusive. Client–Server Architecture defines where processing occurs, Layered Architecture defines how system responsibilities are internally organized, and MVC defines the interaction among the View, Controller, and Model.

### **2.7.5 Suitability of the Software Architectures** {#2.7.5-suitability-of-the-software-architectures}

Based on the comparison, the Smart Bakery Food Waste Reduction System is suitable for adopting a **Layered Client–Server Architecture incorporating the MVC pattern**. Client–Server Architecture separates the Flutter mobile application from the TypeScript backend, centralized database, machine-learning component, and external services. Layered Architecture further organizes these components according to their responsibilities, while MVC separates the Flutter View from the backend Controllers and Models.

This architecture is suitable because it provides clear separation of responsibilities, centralized data management, maintainable business logic, independent module testing, and an appropriate distribution of mobile and server-side processing. The detailed architectural layers, component interactions, and request flow will be presented in Chapter 4 as part of the system design.

## **2.8 Testing Methods** {#2.8-testing-methods}

Software testing determines whether a system functions correctly, satisfies its requirements, and produces reliable results. The Smart Bakery Food Waste Reduction System combines conventional software components with a machine-learning demand-prediction model. Consequently, both software testing and forecasting-model evaluation must be considered. This section reviews software-testing levels, User Acceptance Testing, and evaluation approaches used in bakery demand forecasting. 

### **2.8.1 Software Testing Levels**  {#2.8.1-software-testing-levels}

Common software-testing techniques were reviewed, including white-box, black-box, and grey-box testing, together with unit, integration, system, and acceptance testing [(Tetteh, 2024\)](https://www.researchgate.net/publication/387460992_Software_Testing_Techniques_and_Levels_in_Software_Development). White-box testing examines internal program logic, whereas black-box testing evaluates system inputs and outputs without requiring knowledge of the internal implementation. Grey-box testing combines both perspectives.

Unit testing verifies individual functions, classes, or modules before they are integrated. Integration testing evaluates communication and data exchange among connected components. System testing examines the complete integrated application against its functional and non-functional requirements, while acceptance testing determines whether the software satisfies user and business expectations.

These testing levels are complementary. Unit testing can identify defects within an individual component, but it cannot confirm that multiple modules operate correctly together. Conversely, system testing evaluates complete workflows but may not easily identify the specific component responsible for a defect.

The study provides a useful general framework for software testing. However, it does not address the specialised evaluation requirements of machine-learning systems. A prediction function may execute without software errors while still producing inaccurate forecasts. Therefore, conventional testing must be complemented by forecasting-model evaluation.

### **2.8.2 User Acceptance Testing**  {#2.8.2-user-acceptance-testing}

User Acceptance Testing evaluates whether a completed system supports its intended user activities and satisfies practical requirements. Unlike unit and integration testing, UAT focuses on the suitability of the application from the user’s perspective.

UAT was investigated in Agile-developed applications using collaborative tools and structured test documentation [(Otaduy & Diaz, 2017\)](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.jss.2017.01.002). The study found that continuous customer participation improves requirement validation and allows problems to be identified before final deployment. Asynchronous evaluation also enables participants to test the application at a convenient time and reduces communication barriers.

However, the approach depended on tools such as FitNesse, wikis, and mind maps, which may introduce unnecessary complexity for users with limited technical experience. The study also focused mainly on web applications rather than mobile decision-support systems. Nevertheless, its use of structured scenarios and continuous feedback remains relevant to mobile-system acceptance testing.

### **2.8.3 Bakery Demand-Forecasting Model Evaluation**  {#2.8.3-bakery-demand-forecasting-model-evaluation}

Conventional software testing cannot determine whether a demand-prediction model produces sufficiently accurate forecasts. Forecasting models therefore require quantitative evaluation and comparison with appropriate baseline methods.

Machine-learning methods were evaluated using daily demand data from a German bakery chain [(Huber & Stuckenschmidt, 2020\)](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.ijforecast.2020.02.005). Feed-forward neural networks, recurrent neural networks, and gradient-boosted regression trees were compared with statistical baselines and Linear Regression. The machine-learning methods produced their greatest error reductions, approximately 10% to 20%, on special days and neighbouring days. Recurrent neural networks achieved the strongest overall results, while biweekly model retraining reduced forecast errors by a further 2% to 3%.

The findings demonstrate the importance of evaluating forecasting performance under different calendar conditions rather than relying only on overall average accuracy. The study also shows that retraining frequency can affect model performance. However, its evaluation used aggregated store-category data from a large bakery chain, which may contain less variability than individual product data from a small bakery.

Hierarchical demand forecasting was evaluated using real point-of-sales data from an industrial bakery [(Huber et al., 2017\)](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.eswa.2017.01.022). Their results showed that aggregating substitutable products into meaningful categories reduced data noise. Top-down forecasting also achieved accuracy comparable to direct forecasting while requiring less computational effort.

The study evaluated operational outcomes in addition to statistical forecasting accuracy. Its forecasting approach increased product availability while reducing product losses. This demonstrates that bakery demand forecasting should be evaluated according to both prediction errors and operational consequences. However, the study considered only ARIMA and ARIMAX variants and did not evaluate machine-learning models such as Random Forest.

A review of more than 40 regression and forecasting error measures concluded that no single metric is appropriate for every forecasting problem [(Botchkarev, 2019\)](https://doi.org/10.28945/4184). MAE provides an interpretable average error, RMSE gives greater weight to large errors, MAPE expresses error relative to actual values, and R² indicates the proportion of variation explained by the model. These metrics provide complementary information, although MAPE must be interpreted carefully when actual values are zero or close to zero.

### **2.8.4 Comparison of Testing and Evaluation Approaches**  {#2.8.4-comparison-of-testing-and-evaluation-approaches}

The reviewed literature identifies several approaches that evaluate different aspects of software and prediction quality. Table 2.7 compares these approaches according to their purposes, strengths, limitations, and relevance.

*Table 2.7: Comparison of Testing and Evaluation Approaches*

| Approach | Supporting source | Main purpose | Main strength | Main limitation | Relevance to the proposed project |
| :---- | :---- | :---- | :---- | :---- | :---- |
| Unit testing | [(Tetteh, 2024\)](https://www.researchgate.net/publication/387460992_Software_Testing_Techniques_and_Levels_in_Software_Development) | Verify individual functions and components | Detects defects early and helps identify their source | Does not evaluate interactions among components | Supports verification of individual software functions |
| Integration testing | [(Tetteh, 2024\)](https://www.researchgate.net/publication/387460992_Software_Testing_Techniques_and_Levels_in_Software_Development) | Evaluate interactions and data exchange among connected components | Identifies communication and interface defects | Does not fully evaluate complete user workflows | Supports verification of communication among system components |
| System testing | [(Tetteh, 2024\)](https://www.researchgate.net/publication/387460992_Software_Testing_Techniques_and_Levels_in_Software_Development) | Evaluate the complete integrated application | Verifies complete workflows and system requirements | May not identify the exact source of a defect | Supports overall functional and non-functional validation |
| User Acceptance Testing | [(Otaduy & Diaz, 2017\)](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.jss.2017.01.002) | Determine whether the application satisfies practical user needs | Evaluates usability and requirement satisfaction | Findings depend on participant knowledge and involvement | Supports evaluation from the user’s perspective |
| Forecast-accuracy evaluation | [(Botchkarev, 2019\)](https://doi.org/10.28945/4184),  [(Huber & Stuckenschmidt, 2020\)](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.ijforecast.2020.02.005)  | Measure and compare prediction performance | Provides objective quantitative evidence | High accuracy does not necessarily ensure operational benefits | Supports comparison of forecasting models |
| Special-day and retraining evaluation | [(Huber & Stuckenschmidt, 2020\)](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.ijforecast.2020.02.005)  | Evaluate model reliability under changing calendar and training conditions | Reveals weaknesses that may be hidden by overall results | Requires sufficient data covering different conditions | Supports evaluation of prediction robustness |
| Operational-outcome evaluation | [(Huber et al., 2017\)](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.eswa.2017.01.022)  | Determine whether forecasts improve availability and reduce losses | Connects prediction performance to bakery objectives | Outcomes may be affected by factors beyond the forecasting model | Supports evaluation of food-waste and availability outcomes |

### **2.8.5 Testing Approach for the Proposed Project**  {#2.8.5-testing-approach-for-the-proposed-project}

Based on the comparison, the proposed system will adopt a multi-level testing approach consisting of unit, integration, system, and User Acceptance Testing. The demand-prediction component will also be evaluated using multiple forecasting metrics and operational outcomes. This combination is appropriate because software correctness, prediction accuracy, user suitability, and bakery operational performance cannot be established through a single testing method. Detailed testing procedures, test cases, acceptance criteria, datasets, and results will be presented in the later implementation and testing chapter. 

## **2.9 Mobile Development Frameworks** {#2.9-mobile-development-frameworks}

The selection of a mobile development framework influences application performance, resource consumption, maintainability, code reuse, and development efficiency. The Smart Bakery Food Waste Reduction System requires a mobile interface that can be developed and maintained efficiently by a single developer. Therefore, this section reviews Native Android with Kotlin, Flutter, React Native, and Ionic before selecting the most suitable development framework. 

### **2.9.1 Mobile Development Frameworks**  {#2.9.1-mobile-development-frameworks}

Kotlin, Flutter, and React Native were compared by implementing the same application with each framework [(Suri et al., 2022\)](https://doi.org/10.1145/3590837.3590897). The applications were evaluated according to application size, memory usage, CPU consumption, energy usage, code reusability, and development characteristics.

Native Android with Kotlin achieved the strongest runtime efficiency and produced the smallest application size. However, native development provides less code portability because the implementation is designed specifically for the Android platform.

Flutter provided a balance between runtime performance and development efficiency. Although it required more storage and resources than native Kotlin, it performed more efficiently than React Native in several areas while supporting a shared codebase and consistent interface development. React Native achieved high code reuse but generally required greater CPU resources.

The controlled implementation of the same application strengthened the comparison by reducing differences in functionality. However, the evaluated application was relatively simple and may not fully represent a data-intensive business application involving database communication, reports, prediction results, and external services.

Flutter, React Native, Ionic, and native Android development were compared using execution time, memory consumption, and energy usage [(Oliveira et al., 2023\)](https://doi.org/10.1145/3593434.3593487). Native Android generally provided the strongest resource efficiency. Among the cross-platform frameworks, Flutter demonstrated comparatively low execution-time and energy overhead and performed close to native Android in several CPU-intensive scenarios.

React Native generally required more memory and execution time, while Ionic experienced higher overhead in graphics-intensive operations because it relies on web-based rendering. Nevertheless, the study found that framework performance depends on workload characteristics, meaning that no framework performs best under every condition.

Flutter was further demonstrated to support architectural patterns including MVC, MVVM, MVP, and VIPER [(Neupane & Zhang, 2025\)](https://dl.acm.org/doi/abs/10.5555/3778141.3778148). Their controlled comparison found that MVC provided the lowest structural complexity, highest isolated unit-test coverage, and lowest database-fetch latency. These findings indicate that Flutter provides architectural flexibility, although the selected pattern can affect maintainability, testability, and performance.

### **2.9.2 Comparison of Mobile Development Frameworks**  {#2.9.2-comparison-of-mobile-development-frameworks}

The reviewed frameworks differ in their runtime efficiency, code reuse, development requirements, and platform portability. Table 2.8 compares these characteristics based on the findings of the reviewed studies.

*Table 2.8: Comparison of Mobile Development Frameworks*

| Comparison factor | Native Android (Kotlin) | Flutter | React Native | Ionic |
| :---- | :---- | :---- | :---- | :---- |
| Supporting sources | [(Suri et al., 2022\)](https://doi.org/10.1145/3590837.3590897), [(Oliveira et al., 2023\)](https://doi.org/10.1145/3593434.3593487) | [(Suri et al., 2022\)](https://doi.org/10.1145/3590837.3590897),  [(Oliveira et al., 2023\)](https://doi.org/10.1145/3593434.3593487), [(Neupane & Zhang, 2025\)](https://dl.acm.org/doi/abs/10.5555/3778141.3778148) | [(Suri et al., 2022\)](https://doi.org/10.1145/3590837.3590897),  [(Oliveira et al., 2023\)](https://doi.org/10.1145/3593434.3593487) | [(Oliveira et al., 2023\)](https://doi.org/10.1145/3593434.3593487) |
| Development approach | Native Android development | Cross-platform development using Dart | Cross-platform development using JavaScript or TypeScript | Hybrid development using web technologies |
| Runtime efficiency | Highest overall resource efficiency | Comparatively close to native performance in several scenarios | Higher CPU, memory, and execution overhead in several tests | Greater overhead, particularly in graphics-intensive operations |
| Code reuse | Limited when extending the application to other platforms | High code reuse through a shared codebase | High code reuse through a shared codebase | High reuse of HTML, CSS, and JavaScript |
| Interface consistency | Uses native Android interface components | Provides consistent interfaces through Flutter widgets | Depends partly on platform components and framework implementation | Interfaces are rendered through web technologies |
| Main strengths | Strong performance, small application size, and direct access to Android features | Good performance, shared codebase, consistent interface design, and flexible architectural support | High code reuse and a broad JavaScript ecosystem | Rapid development for developers familiar with web technologies |
| Main limitations | Platform-specific and less portable to other operating systems | Larger application size and some runtime overhead compared with native development | Greater resource consumption in several evaluated scenarios | Higher graphics and WebView-related overhead |
| Suitability for the proposed project | Suitable for Android performance but provides limited future portability | Highly suitable because it balances performance, maintainability, and development efficiency | Suitable, but the evaluated resource overhead is less favourable | Less suitable for a data-intensive mobile application requiring consistent performance |

Native Android with Kotlin provides the strongest runtime and resource efficiency. It is appropriate when maximum Android-specific performance is the main requirement. However, its platform-specific implementation provides less portability and may require separate development if the system is extended to other platforms.

React Native and Ionic provide high code reuse and rapid development. However, the reviewed studies identified greater resource overhead in several scenarios. Ionic’s reliance on web-based rendering may also be less suitable for applications requiring consistent mobile-interface performance.

Flutter does not always match the resource efficiency of native Android, but it provides a stronger balance among runtime performance, shared-code development, interface consistency, and maintainability. Its support for different architectural patterns also allows its internal structure to be adapted according to project complexity.

### **2.9.3 Selected Development Framework**  {#2.9.3-selected-development-framework}

Based on the comparison, **Flutter with Dart** is selected as the mobile development framework for the Smart Bakery Food Waste Reduction System. Flutter provides acceptable runtime efficiency while supporting rapid interface development, a consistent widget-based interface, and a maintainable shared codebase.

These characteristics are suitable for a single-developer project and provide potential portability if the application is extended beyond Android in the future. The detailed Flutter structure, packages, backend communication, and supporting technologies will be explained in the later design and implementation chapters.

## **2.10 Related Works** {#2.10-related-works}

Previous bakery-related studies have applied demand forecasting, production scheduling, and production planning techniques to reduce overproduction, improve resource utilization, and support operational decision-making. However, these works generally focus on individual business problems rather than providing a fully integrated intelligent bakery management system. This section reviews three related works and compares their contributions with the proposed Smart Bakery Food Waste Reduction System.

### **2.10.1 Machine-Learning-Based Bakery Demand Forecasting** {#2.10.1-machine-learning-based-bakery-demand-forecasting}

Foodforecast, a commercial machine-learning demand forecasting service implemented across German bakeries, was evaluated [(Hübner et al., 2024)](https://doi.org/10.1111/jiec.13528). The study examined whether the environmental benefits obtained through reduced bakery returns outweighed the environmental impacts of operating the forecasting service.

The results showed that Foodforecast reduced average bakery return weight by approximately 30% across 175 bakeries. Historical sales data and machine learning enabled bakeries to estimate demand more accurately, improve production planning, and reduce unnecessary overproduction. The environmental benefits produced through avoiding food waste were considerably greater than the environmental costs associated with running the machine-learning infrastructure.

A major strength of the study is its use of real operational data from a large number of bakeries, providing practical evidence that machine-learning-based demand forecasting can reduce bakery returns and food waste. However, the study focuses mainly on forecasting outcomes and environmental evaluation, offering limited information about the forecasting algorithms, software architecture, operational features, and integration of Foodforecast with other bakery operations. 

### **2.10.2 Forecasting and Master Production Scheduling** {#2.10.2-forecasting-and-master-production-scheduling}

Production planning was investigated at Soku Bakery by combining historical demand forecasting with Master Production Scheduling [(Dendy et al., 2022\)](https://doi.org/10.46254/eu05.20220240). The study applied the Simple Moving Average method to estimate future demand and used the forecasting results to determine suitable production quantities.

The findings showed that combining demand forecasting with a Master Production Schedule improved production planning, reduced excessive inventory, minimized the likelihood of expired bakery products, and supported timely fulfilment of customer demand. The approach was particularly suitable for a micro-business because it was relatively simple and could be applied using historical sales records.

Unlike Foodforecast, which applied machine learning, the Soku Bakery study relied on a traditional statistical forecasting method. The Simple Moving Average is easy to implement and interpret, but it may not capture nonlinear demand patterns or the influence of weather, holidays, seasonality, and other contextual variables. The study also focused mainly on determining production quantities and did not present a complete intelligent software platform.

Nevertheless, the study demonstrates that forecasting becomes more operationally valuable when it is connected to production scheduling. This finding is relevant to the proposed system, which transforms predicted demand into production recommendations after considering ingredient availability and operational constraints.

### **2.10.3 Production Planning and Control in Bakery SMEs** {#2.10.3-production-planning-and-control-in-bakery-smes}

The application of Production Planning and Control concepts was examined in a small bakery company [(Mamat et al., 2022\)](https://doi.org/10.15282/ijim.16.1.2022.9006). The study applied the Quantity Discount Model to supplier and purchasing decisions and used Aggregate Planning to evaluate whether workforce capacity was sufficient to meet forecasted demand.

The results showed that structured planning methods could identify more cost-effective suppliers, determine appropriate purchasing quantities, and reveal workforce shortages. Aligning production capacity with demand reduced the risk of failing to fulfil customer orders and improved overall operational efficiency.

This study contributes an operational perspective that is less prominent in the previous two works. Foodforecast mainly addresses demand prediction, while the Soku Bakery study connects forecasting with production scheduling. Mamat et al. (2022) extend the discussion to purchasing, supplier selection, and workforce capacity.

However, the study relies on traditional planning calculations and does not present a machine-learning-enabled software system. Its main contribution concerns purchasing, supplier selection, workforce capacity, and production planning. 

### **2.10.4 Comparison of Related Works** {#2.10.4-comparison-of-related-works}

The three related works address different aspects of bakery planning and food-waste reduction.

*Table 2.9: Comparison of Related Works* 

| Comparison factor | Foodforecast | Soku Bakery | Bakery SME PPC study | Proposed system |
| :---- | :---- | :---- | :---- | :---- |
| Bakery demand forecasting | Yes | Yes | Uses forecasted demand | Yes |
| Machine learning | Yes | Not applied | Not applied | Yes |
| Traditional forecasting | Not clearly described | Simple Moving Average | Supporting forecasts | Linear Regression baseline |
| External factors | Limited public detail | Not reported | Not reported | Weather, holidays, temporal patterns |
| Production scheduling or recommendation | Forecast-supported planning | Master Production Schedule | Aggregate planning | Inventory-aware recommendation |
| Ingredient inventory management | Not clearly described | Limited | Purchasing-focused | Yes |
| Supplier or workforce planning | Not reported | Not reported | Yes | Outside the current scope |
| POS simulation | Not reported | Not reported | Not reported | Yes |
| Lost-sales estimation | Not reported | Not reported | Capacity shortage only | Yes |
| Leftover and donation management | Not reported | Not reported | Not reported | Yes |
| Reporting dashboard | Not clearly described | Limited | Limited | Yes |
| Alerts and notifications | Not clearly described | Not reported | Not reported | Yes |
| Mobile application | Not clearly described | No integrated app | No integrated app | Yes |

The related works agree that bakery performance improves when forecasting and production decisions are supported by operational data. Foodforecast provides practical evidence that machine learning can reduce bakery returns. The Soku Bakery study demonstrates that forecasts become more useful when connected to production scheduling, while the Bakery SME PPC study highlights the importance of purchasing and capacity considerations. Collectively, these findings support combining demand prediction with production and inventory decision support in the proposed project. 

## **2.11 Chapter Summary** {#2.11-chapter-summary}

This chapter reviewed the proposed project from domain, analytical, software-engineering, and technology perspectives. The bakery food-waste literature consistently identifies overproduction, weak demand information, process errors, and limited coordination as major causes of loss. Prevention through better forecasting and production planning is generally preferable to handling surplus after production, although donation and recovery remain necessary for unavoidable leftovers.

The forecasting literature shows that advanced models such as XGBoost and recurrent neural networks can achieve high accuracy, but they require greater data volume, tuning effort, and implementation complexity. Random Forest provides a more suitable balance for a small-bakery decision-support system because it can model nonlinear relationships and multiple contextual features while remaining comparatively manageable. Linear Regression provides an interpretable baseline, and multiple metrics are required to evaluate model performance fairly.

The software-engineering review supports an Agile approach with structured initial planning, complementary requirements methods, object-oriented and modular design, and a layered client–server architecture supported by MVC. The testing literature further shows that system quality cannot be established through one method alone; unit, integration, system/end-to-end, user acceptance, non-functional, and machine-learning evaluation address different risks.

The related works demonstrate that machine-learning forecasting, master production scheduling, and production-planning methods can support bakery operations by improving demand estimation, resource allocation, and production decisions. Each work contributes insights into particular operational areas, including forecasting, scheduling, environmental evaluation, supplier decisions, and workforce capacity. Collectively, these findings support the integration of demand prediction with practical bakery-management functions in the proposed system.

Drawing on these findings, the Smart Bakery Food Waste Reduction System adopts an integrated but deliberately manageable scope that connects next-day demand prediction with ingredient and recipe constraints, manager-confirmed production quantities, sales simulation, lost-sales estimation, leftover and donation management, dashboards, and alerts. Major operations are initiated manually by the manager, making the decision-making process visible and controllable while avoiding reliance on background scheduling. The findings reviewed in this chapter provide the foundation for the Agile methodology and requirements analysis discussed in Chapter 3, as well as the architecture and detailed system design presented in Chapter 4\.

Chapter 3

**Methodology and Requirements Analysis**

# **3 Methodology and Requirements Analysis** {#3-methodology-and-requirements-analysis}

## **3.1 Introduction** {#3.1-introduction}

This chapter presents the development methodology and requirements analysis for the Smart Bakery Food Waste Reduction System. Agile is adopted as the development methodology because it supports incremental development, continuous testing, regular feedback, and iterative refinement. These characteristics are suitable for the proposed system because its functional modules, mobile interfaces, machine-learning model, production-recommendation rules, and external-service integrations may require improvement throughout the development process. The chapter also explains how the Agile stages are tailored to the scope, schedule, and single-developer structure of the project.

The requirements-gathering process applies document analysis and prototyping to identify and refine the system requirements. Document analysis provides an understanding of bakery operations, food-waste problems, demand forecasting, inventory constraints, and related systems, while prototyping supports the visualization and evaluation of the proposed mobile interfaces and operational workflows. The identified requirements are subsequently analysed using appropriate models, including system context, and use case. Detailed functional and non-functional requirements are then specified to define the expected system behaviour and quality characteristics. Together, these requirements establish a structured foundation for the system architecture and detailed design presented in Chapter 4\.

## **3.2 Development Methodology**  {#3.2-development-methodology}

A development methodology provides a structured process for planning, developing, testing, reviewing, and improving a software system. Based on the methodology comparison presented in Section 2.4, Agile is selected for the development of the Smart Bakery Food Waste Reduction System. The selected approach supports incremental implementation while allowing requirements, interfaces, prediction features, and operational workflows to be refined based on testing and feedback.

The proposed project applies a tailored Agile process rather than adopting every practice from a specific Agile framework such as Scrum. This is appropriate because the project is developed by a single developer and does not involve a conventional development team with separate Scrum roles. Nevertheless, the project retains the principal Agile characteristics of iterative development, continuous testing, regular review, incremental delivery, and responsiveness to change.

### **3.2.1 Agile Development Methodology**  {#3.2.1-agile-development-methodology}

Agile is an iterative and incremental development approach in which a system is developed through a series of manageable increments. Each increment involves selecting requirements, designing and developing the relevant functions, testing the implementation, obtaining feedback, and refining the resulting system. Instead of completing the entire system before evaluation, Agile allows functional components to be reviewed and improved throughout development.

The Agile Manifesto emphasizes working software, stakeholder collaboration, and responsiveness to change, while its principles support frequent delivery and continuous improvement [(Beck et al., 2001\)](https://agilemanifesto.org). An analysis of 1,002 projects identified a positive relationship between the application of Agile practices and project success, including project efficiency and stakeholder satisfaction [(Serrador & Pinto, 2015\)](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.ijproman.2015.01.006). Their findings support the use of iterative planning and continuous feedback rather than relying entirely on a fixed development process established at the beginning of a project.

Agile is suitable for the Smart Bakery Food Waste Reduction System because the system consists of eight functional modules that can be developed and evaluated incrementally. These modules include User and Access Management, Demand Prediction, Inventory and Smart Production Recommendation, POS and Sales Simulation, Leftover, Donation and Waste Management, Reporting and Dashboard, Alerts and Notifications, and System Administration. Developing these modules incrementally reduces implementation complexity and allows problems within individual modules to be identified before full system integration.

The methodology is also appropriate for the machine-learning component. Demand prediction involves data preparation, feature generation, model training, evaluation, confidence calculation, and comparison between Random Forest Regression and Linear Regression. The results of model evaluation may reveal the need to modify input features, model parameters, data-validation rules, or prediction-presentation methods. Agile allows these activities to be repeated until the model produces sufficiently reliable and understandable results.

Similarly, prototyping and continuous review allow the mobile interfaces and operational workflows to be refined. For example, feedback may reveal that prediction confidence is unclear, the production-recommendation workflow requires additional explanation, or the manager needs more information before overriding a recommendation. These findings can be incorporated into subsequent increments without changing the overall project objectives.

Although Agile allows requirements to be refined, the principal project scope and objectives remain controlled. Features outside the approved scope, including customer ordering, payment processing, delivery services, real POS integration, multi-branch management, and automatic background scheduling, will not be added merely as part of iterative development. Therefore, Agile provides flexibility within the approved project scope rather than permitting uncontrolled expansion.

### **3.2.2 Tailored Agile Development Process**  {#3.2.2-tailored-agile-development-process}

The Agile process is tailored to the scope, schedule, and single-developer structure of the Smart Bakery Food Waste Reduction System. It begins with initial planning and requirements gathering, followed by requirement prioritization and iteration planning. Selected requirements are then designed, developed, integrated, and tested. The resulting increment is reviewed based on test findings, prototype feedback, and supervisor evaluation. Identified changes are returned to the requirements backlog and addressed in a subsequent iteration. This process continues until all planned modules have been implemented, integrated, and evaluated. 

![][image5]  
*Figure 3.1: Tailored Agile Development Process for the Smart Bakery Food Waste Reduction System*

*Table 3.1: Stages of the Tailored Agile Development Process* 

| Stage | Strategy | Application in the proposed project | Main output |
| :---- | :---- | :---- | :---- |
| Initial planning and requirements | Document analysis and low-fidelity prototyping | Establish the objectives, scope, constraints, stakeholders and initial requirements | Initial requirements |
| Prioritised requirements backlog | Dependency-based prioritisation | Organise requirements according to module, importance and development dependency | Prioritised requirements backlog |
| Iteration planning | Incremental planning | Select related requirements that can be implemented and evaluated as one manageable increment | Development increment plan specifying the selected modules, activities and expected deliverables (see Table 3.2).  |
| Design and prototyping | Modular and object-oriented design; prototyping | Prepare interface prototypes, workflows, data structures and technical designs | Approved design or prototype |
| Development and integration | Incremental development and integration | Implement the selected mobile, backend, database, machine-learning and external-service functions | Integrated system functions |
| Testing and evaluation | Unit, integration and machine-learning evaluation | Test the completed functions and prediction models | Test and evaluation results |
| Review and feedback | Supervisor review and prototype feedback | Review the increment based on test findings and evaluator feedback | Feedback and change requests |
| Refinement | Backlog refinement and defect correction | Correct defects and refine requirements, interfaces, rules and model features | Improved requirements and system |
| Working system increment |  | Confirm that the selected functions operate correctly before continuing | Verified system increment |
| Final system evaluation | System testing and UAT | Integrate all increments and evaluate the complete system | Evaluated final system |

### **3.2.3 Application of Agile to the Proposed Project** {#3.2.3-application-of-agile-to-the-proposed-project}

The proposed system will be implemented through six major development increments. The order of the increments considers functional dependencies. For example, user authentication and administrative data must be available before protected operational functions are developed. Similarly, demand prediction and inventory information must be available before an inventory-aware production recommendation can be generated. 

*Table 3.2: Planned Development Increments* 

| Increment | Main modules and activities | Expected output |
| :---- | :---- | :---- |
| 1: System foundation | Development environment, database, User and Access Management, System Administration and external-service configuration | Secure and configurable system foundation |
| 2: Demand prediction | Data preparation, feature generation, cold-start method, Random Forest model, Linear Regression baseline, confidence assessment and model evaluation | Working next-day demand-prediction component |
| 3: Inventory and production planning | Ingredients, bread categories, recipes, FIFO inventory, inventory validation, production-feasibility checking and production recommendations | Inventory-aware production-planning component |
| 4: Sales simulation | Production-decision retrieval, contextual sales simulation, stock-limited transactions, lost-sales calculation and end-of-day aggregation | Working POS and sales-simulation component |
| 5: Surplus and monitoring | Leftover calculation, donation and waste management, dashboards, reports, alerts and notifications | Operational monitoring and surplus-management functions |
| 6: Integration and evaluation | Complete module integration, defect correction, system testing, machine-learning evaluation and User Acceptance Testing | Integrated and evaluated final system |

Within each increment, the selected requirements will be designed, implemented, tested, and reviewed. Any defects, unclear requirements, unsuitable interfaces, or inaccurate model behaviour identified during evaluation will be recorded and addressed through refinement. This iterative process allows the system to improve progressively while ensuring that each completed increment remains aligned with the project objectives and approved scope. 

## **3.3 Requirements Gathering Techniques** {#3.3-requirements-gathering-techniques}

Requirements gathering, also referred to as requirements elicitation, is conducted to identify the functions, data, business rules, constraints, user interactions, and quality expectations of the proposed system. The requirements-gathering process must provide sufficient information to define what the system should perform while ensuring that the identified requirements remain consistent with the project objectives and scope.

Based on the comparison presented in Section 2.5, Document Analysis and Prototyping are selected as complementary requirements-gathering techniques for the Smart Bakery Food Waste Reduction System. Document Analysis is used to establish the initial understanding of bakery food-waste problems, demand forecasting, inventory constraints, surplus management, and relevant system functions. Prototyping is subsequently used to visualize and refine the proposed mobile interfaces and operational workflows. The requirements obtained through these techniques are consolidated and validated before being presented as formal functional and non-functional requirements.

### **3.3.1 Document Analysis** {#3.3.1-document-analysis}

Document Analysis was applied as the initial requirements-gathering technique. This technique identifies requirements by examining existing materials related to a business domain, operational process, problem, or software solution. Document Analysis was commonly applied by software practitioners, particularly when developers needed to understand unfamiliar business environments and existing systems [(Huchenko & Gobov, 2020\)](https://doi.org/10.15439/2020f16).

For the proposed system, the analysed materials included the project proposal, bakery food-waste literature, demand-forecasting studies, related bakery systems, descriptions of bakery workflows, representative sales and inventory data structures, recipe and ingredient information, technical documentation, and supervisor feedback. These materials provided information about the causes of bakery food waste, the factors affecting customer demand, inventory and recipe constraints, leftover-management practices, suitable machine-learning models, and the limitations of existing bakery-management approaches.

The main materials analysed and the requirements derived from them are summarised in Table 3.3.

*Table 3.3: Application of Document Analysis in Requirements Gathering*

| Analysed material | Information identified | Requirements derived |
| :---- | :---- | :---- |
| Project proposal and Chapter 1 project scope | Project objectives, system boundaries, functional modules, target platform and excluded features | Requirements must support a single-bakery Android application and exclude online ordering, payment, delivery, multi-branch management and automatic background scheduling |
| Bakery food-waste literature | Overproduction, uncertain demand, short shelf life, production losses and unavoidable surplus | Demand prediction, production planning, leftover calculation, donation management and waste tracking |
| Demand-forecasting studies | Historical sales patterns, temporal factors, weather, public holidays, forecasting models and evaluation measurements | Predictive data preparation, Random Forest Regression, Linear Regression baseline, confidence assessment and model evaluation |
| Bakery workflows and related systems | Daily production planning, sales recording, inventory monitoring and surplus handling | Manager-initiated production decisions, sales simulation, inventory management, reporting and surplus-management workflows |
| Recipe and ingredient structures | Relationships between bread categories, recipes, ingredient quantities and available stock | Recipe management, FIFO inventory, production-feasibility checking and maximum-producible-quantity calculation |
| Sales and transaction structures | Product quantities, selling prices, transaction times, revenue, lost sales and estimated demand | Sales-transaction recording, stock-limited simulation, financial snapshots and end-of-day aggregation |
| Related bakery studies and systems | Existing solutions commonly focus on individual forecasting or production-planning problems | Integration of prediction, inventory-aware recommendations, simulation, surplus management, reporting and alerts |
| External-service documentation | Availability of weather, public-holiday and notification information | External-data retrieval, configuration, error handling and notification-delivery requirements |
| Supervisor feedback | Major operations should remain visible and controllable by the manager | Prediction generation, model retraining, production confirmation and sales simulation must be manually initiated |

The identified information was organized according to the eight functional modules of the proposed system. Duplicate requirements were combined, requirements outside the approved project scope were excluded, and unclear requirements were refined into more specific system functions. For example, the general need for improved production planning was refined into separate requirements for demand prediction, recipe-based ingredient calculation, production-feasibility checking, recommendation generation, and manager confirmation.

Document Analysis provides traceable information and is suitable for the project because direct access to extensive bakery stakeholders and operational records is limited. However, documents alone cannot fully demonstrate whether the proposed interfaces, terminology, navigation, and user interactions are clear. Therefore, Prototyping is used as a complementary technique to visualize and refine the initial requirements.

### **3.3.2 Prototyping** {#3.3.2-prototyping}

Prototyping is used to create an early representation of the proposed system before complete implementation. Prototypes allow proposed functions and interactions to be visualized, helping to identify missing, unclear, or unsuitable requirements [(Pacheco et al., 2018\)](https://doi.org/10.1049/iet-sen.2017.0144). Paper Prototyping was effective in identifying functional requirements while requiring a manageable amount of preparation time [(Rueda et al., 2020\)](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.infsof.2020.106361).

For this project, low-fidelity prototypes will first be prepared to represent the principal Android application screens and navigation paths. These prototypes focus on the information displayed, user actions, workflow sequence, terminology, and navigation rather than complete visual styling or backend implementation. The prototype screens and their validation purposes are presented in Table 3.4.

*Table 3.4: Proposed Prototype Screens and Validation Purposes*

| Prototype screen or workflow | Main elements represented | Requirements to be validated |
| :---- | :---- | :---- |
| Login and profile | Login fields, authentication feedback, profile information and logout function | Authentication, session management and profile-management requirements |
| Main dashboard | Summary cards, alerts, navigation and pending-action indicators | Information visibility, navigation and notification requirements |
| Demand prediction | Prediction initiation, predicted quantity, confidence level, demand factors and model information | Prediction, confidence, explanation and manual-initiation requirements |
| Production recommendation | Predicted demand, available ingredients, limiting ingredients, recommended quantity and decision options | Production-feasibility and manager-decision requirements |
| Inventory management | Ingredient information, inventory batches, expiry dates, reorder levels and stock movements | Ingredient, FIFO inventory, low-stock and inventory-validation requirements |
| Sales simulation | Simulation initiation, contextual information, progress and end-of-day results | Manual simulation, stock-limited sales, lost-sales and aggregation requirements |
| Leftover and donation management | Leftover quantities, charity selection, donation status and waste reasons | Leftover, donation and waste-management requirements |
| Reporting and dashboard | Prediction, inventory, sales, waste, donation and estimated financial information | Dashboard, weekly reporting and report-export requirements |
| Notification centre | Alert category, date, read status and related record | In-application notification and notification-history requirements |
| Administration | Users, bread categories, recipes, system parameters, services and audit records | Administration, configuration and access-control requirements |

The prototypes will be reviewed to determine whether the system’s information and workflows are understandable and complete. Particular attention will be given to whether the manager can clearly distinguish predicted demand from recommended production, understand prediction confidence, identify ingredient shortages, and accept, reduce, or override a recommendation. The prototypes will also be used to verify that manager-initiated operations are clearly presented and are not mistaken for automatically scheduled processes.

Feedback will be recorded according to the affected screen or workflow, the identified problem, the corresponding requirement, and the action taken. Accepted changes will be reflected in the functional requirements, use case descriptions, and subsequent system design. A working prototype will later be developed using the refined low-fidelity interfaces and reviewed during the planned prototype-evaluation stage.

### **3.3.3 Requirements Consolidation and Validation**  {#3.3.3-requirements-consolidation-and-validation}

The initial requirements identified through Document Analysis will be consolidated into a requirements list. Prototyping will subsequently be used to validate and refine these requirements during the design and development stages. During consolidation, overlapping requirements will be combined, inconsistent terminology will be standardised, and broad requirements will be divided into smaller and more testable statements. 

The consolidated requirements are validated according to the following criteria:

*Table 3.5: Criteria of Consolidated Requirement Validation*

| Validation criterion | Application in the proposed project |
| :---- | :---- |
| Alignment | Every requirement must support at least one project objective, functional module or operational need |
| Completeness | All eight functional modules and important workflows must be represented |
| Consistency | Requirements must use consistent actors, module names, calculation rules and terminology |
| Feasibility | Requirements must be achievable within the available time, technology, hardware and single-developer structure |
| Clarity | Each requirement must describe a specific system behaviour without ambiguous expressions |
| Testability | Functional and non-functional requirements must be capable of verification during system testing or User Acceptance Testing |
| Traceability | Requirements must be traceable to the project scope, analysed material, prototype feedback or supervisor feedback |
| Scope control | Requirements involving excluded functions must not be included in the development backlog |

The validation process also ensures that prediction generation, model retraining, production confirmation, and sales simulation remain manually initiated by authorised users. Event-based notifications may be delivered in the background, but they do not automatically execute these operational processes. This distinction prevents the requirements from conflicting with the approved removal of automatic scheduling.

Once consolidated and validated, the requirements provide the basis for the stakeholder analysis, use case models, and formal requirements specifications presented in the following sections.

## **3.4 Requirements Analysis** {#3.4-requirements-analysis}

Requirements analysis transforms the information obtained during requirements gathering into a structured description of the proposed system. It identifies the stakeholders and actors, establishes the system boundary, analyses the interactions between users and the system, and defines the workflows and business rules that control system behaviour. This process helps ensure that the proposed requirements are complete, consistent, feasible, and aligned with the project objectives.

The requirements analysis for the Smart Bakery Food Waste Reduction System applies stakeholder and actor analysis, a system context diagram, use-case diagrams and business rules. The system context diagram establishes the system boundary, while the use-case diagrams describe the functions and interactions available to each actor. The analysis also defines important business rules governing prediction, inventory, production recommendations, sales simulation, and surplus management.

### **3.4.1 Stakeholder and Actor Analysis**  {#3.4.1-stakeholder-and-actor-analysis}

Stakeholders are individuals or groups who influence, develop, evaluate, operate, or are affected by the proposed system. An actor is a stakeholder or external system that directly interacts with the application. The principal stakeholders and actors are presented in Table 3.6.

*Table 3.6: Stakeholders and Actors of the Proposed System*

| Stakeholder or actor | Type | Responsibilities or interests | Direct system interaction |
| :---- | :---- | :---- | :---- |
| Bakery Manager | Primary actor | Make daily production decisions, generate predictions, review recommendations, run sales simulations, manage surplus, and monitor bakery performance | Yes |
| System Administrator | Primary actor | Manage users, ingredients, bread categories, recipes, charity partners, system parameters, external-service configuration, and audit information | Yes |
| Project Supervisor | Stakeholder | Review the project scope, requirements, methodology, design, progress, and academic suitability | No |
| System Developer | Stakeholder | Analyse, design, implement, test, deploy, and document the proposed system | No operational interaction |
| Selected Evaluators | Stakeholders | Evaluate the usability and suitability of the completed application during User Acceptance Testing | During evaluation only |
| Weather Service | Supporting actor | Provide weather conditions required for prediction and sales simulation | Yes |
| Calendar/Holiday Service | Supporting actor | Provide Malaysian calendar and holiday information | Yes |
| Push Notification Service | Supporting actor | Deliver event-based background notifications to authorised users | Yes |

The Bakery Manager and System Administrator are modelled as separate roles because their responsibilities and permissions are different. The manager is responsible for operational decisions, while the administrator manages master data, users, configurations and system controls. Each user account is assigned exactly one role, either Bakery Manager or System Administrator. An account cannot hold both roles simultaneously, and access to system functions is restricted according to its assigned role.

Both roles are considered authenticated users and can perform common functions such as logging in, logging out, managing their profiles, viewing permitted notifications, and accessing authorised information. A charity partner is not modelled as a system actor because charity organizations do not directly log in to or operate the proposed application. Their information and donation status are recorded by an authorised system user.

### **3.4.2 System Context Analysis**   {#3.4.2-system-context-analysis}

The system context diagram defines the boundary of the Smart Bakery Food Waste Reduction System and shows its interactions with human actors and external services.
