| NFR-ACC-08 | Prediction confidence | The system shall display a numerical confidence indicator for every model-based prediction and label it as Low Confidence when the indicator is below the configured threshold, initially 75%. Cold-start predictions shall be separately identified as low-confidence heuristic estimates without displaying a numerical confidence value.  | Prediction and notification testing |

The non-functional requirements establish measurable quality expectations for the proposed system. Performance requirements ensure that operational functions respond within an acceptable period, while security and reliability requirements protect the system and its data from unauthorised access, incomplete processing and external-service failures. Usability, maintainability, compatibility and data-integrity requirements further ensure that the system can be operated effectively, tested systematically and enhanced during future development. MAE is selected as the primary model-comparison metric because it expresses the average prediction error in the original unit of bread quantity and is relatively straightforward to interpret. RMSE, MAPE and R² are used as complementary metrics to provide a more comprehensive evaluation. 

## **3.7 Chapter Summary** {#3.7-chapter-summary}

This chapter presented the development methodology and requirements analysis for the proposed Smart Bakery Food Waste Reduction System. A tailored Agile methodology was selected because it supports iterative development, continuous refinement and frequent evaluation of individual system modules. The methodology divides development into manageable iterations covering planning, design, implementation, testing, review and refinement. This is suitable for the project because the demand-prediction, inventory, POS simulation, leftover-management and reporting functions can be developed and evaluated incrementally.

Document analysis and prototyping were selected as the primary requirements-gathering techniques. Document analysis was used to examine the project objectives, bakery operational processes, related systems and findings from the literature review. Prototyping will be used during development to present important interfaces and workflows for early evaluation. The gathered requirements will continue to be refined during the Agile iterations when usability issues, technical limitations or missing requirements are identified.

The requirements analysis identified the Bakery Manager and System Administrator as the main human actors, while the Weather Service, Calendar/Holiday Service and Push Notification Service were identified as supporting external systems. The system context diagram established the system boundary, while the use case diagrams described the functions available to each actor. Detailed use case specifications documented the main and alternative flows of the major processes. Implementation-oriented activity diagrams for the major system workflows are presented in Chapter 4 as part of the detailed system design. 

Business rules were established to control model usage, production feasibility, FIFO inventory processing, simulation calculations and leftover allocation. The functional requirements define the services that the system shall provide, while the non-functional requirements establish measurable expectations for performance, security, reliability, usability, maintainability, compatibility, data integrity and prediction quality. Prediction quality will be evaluated using MAE, RMSE, MAPE and R², with Linear Regression serving as the baseline for comparison with the Random Forest model.

Overall, the requirements analysis provides a structured and traceable foundation for the subsequent design and development of the proposed system. The requirements are aligned with the project objectives and support a manually initiated operational workflow without relying on automated scheduling. The next chapter presents the system design used to translate these requirements into the proposed architecture, data structures, interfaces and component interactions. 

Chapter 4

**System Design**

# **4 System Design** {#4-system-design}

## **4.1 Introduction** {#4.1-introduction}

This chapter presents the detailed system design of the Smart Bakery Food Waste Reduction System based on the requirements and business rules established in Chapter 3\. The purpose of the system design is to translate the identified requirements into an implementable technical structure that guides the subsequent development and integration of the system components. The design follows the selected Modular Design strategy, supported by Object-Oriented Design principles, to separate the system into manageable functional modules with clearly defined responsibilities.

The proposed system adopts a Layered Client-Server Architecture incorporating the Model View Controller pattern. The architecture separates the Flutter mobile interface, TypeScript controllers and business services, Python machine-learning services, data-access components, Supabase data services and supporting external services. This separation supports maintainability, controlled data access, independent module testing and the integration of resource-intensive prediction processing outside the mobile application.

This chapter presents the software architecture, object-oriented and modular design, process and interaction design, database design, user-interface design, report and dashboard design, and the algorithms used for demand prediction, production recommendation, FIFO inventory processing, POS simulation and leftover management. It also explains the security, reliability, performance, usability, maintainability, data-integrity and prediction-quality mechanisms incorporated into the design to address the non-functional requirements of the proposed system.

## **4.2 Software Architecture Design** {#4.2-software-architecture-design}

### **4.2.1 Architectural Overview**  {#4.2.1-architectural-overview}

The Smart Bakery Food Waste Reduction System adopts a **Layered Client–Server Architecture incorporating the Model–View–Controller (MVC) pattern**. Client–Server Architecture separates the Flutter mobile application from server-side processing and data services. Layered Architecture organises responsibilities into presentation, application, business, data-access and database layers, while MVC separates interface presentation, request handling and data representation. The architecture primarily addresses the architecturally significant requirements of maintainability, security, reliability, data integrity and performance identified in Section 3.6.

Maintainability is particularly important because the prediction model, production-recommendation rules and mobile interfaces may require repeated refinement during Agile development. Separating controllers, business services, repositories and machine-learning processing allows changes to be concentrated within the relevant component, supporting NFR-MAI-01. For example, prediction algorithms can be modified within the Python/FastAPI service without directly changing the Flutter interface, provided that the API contract remains compatible. These boundaries also support independent component testing.

Security and data integrity influence the decision to centralise protected business operations in the TypeScript backend. The backend validates authentication and role permissions before processing requests, while repositories provide controlled database access. Sensitive service credentials remain on the server rather than in the mobile application. These decisions support NFR-SEC-01, NFR-SEC-02 and NFR-SEC-05. Database transactions and validation constraints support NFR-REL-01 and NFR-DAT-01 by preventing incomplete or invalid inventory, simulation and leftover-allocation updates.

Performance requirements also influence the distribution of responsibilities. Machine-learning processing is performed by the FastAPI service rather than on the Android device. Indexed queries, pagination and contextual-data caching are intended to support the response-time targets in NFR-PER-01 to NFR-PER-03 under the defined reference environment. However, separating processing between components does not guarantee these targets; performance testing is required. Reliability is supported through controlled external-service error handling and preservation of the active prediction model when retraining fails, addressing NFR-REL-02 and NFR-REL-03.

The architecture introduces several trade-offs. Additional layers, repositories and API contracts increase implementation and integration effort for a single developer. Communication between the mobile application, backend and external services adds latency and creates dependence on network and service availability. Hosting Express and FastAPI as separate processes on one application server simplifies deployment, but a server-wide failure can affect both services. The design therefore balances maintainability and controlled processing against development complexity, communication overhead and availability limitations. To keep this balance appropriate for a single-bakery project, the business modules remain within one Express backend, with only the specialised machine-learning processing separated into FastAPI

Figure 4.1 presents the overall architecture of the proposed system. The horizontal boundaries represent the architectural layers, while the Server-Side Components boundary groups the components that perform backend and machine-learning processing. The Node.js/Express TypeScript backend and Python/FastAPI machine-learning service are shown as separate server-side services. They may operate as separate processes using different ports, even when deployed on the same physical or cloud server.

![][image10]  
*Figure 4.1: Layered Client–Server Architecture Incorporating the MVC Pattern*

The Presentation Layer contains the Flutter Android mobile application, which represents the **View** of the MVC pattern. It provides screens, widgets, navigation controls and an API client through which the Bakery Manager and System Administrator interact with the system. The View presents information received from the backend and collects user input, but it does not directly implement the main business rules, database operations or machine-learning processing.

Supabase Authentication supports user login, session management and authentication-token issuance. After successful authentication, the Flutter application includes the issued JSON Web Token in protected requests sent to the TypeScript backend. The TypeScript API controllers validate the token and retrieve the authenticated user information through Supabase Authentication where required. Supabase Realtime delivers secure in-application notification events to the Flutter application using a secure WebSocket connection.

The Application Layer contains the TypeScript API controllers, which represent the **Controller** of the MVC pattern. The controllers receive HTTPS REST API requests from the Flutter application, validate the supplied information, verify authentication and role permissions, and delegate valid requests to the appropriate TypeScript business service. The controllers subsequently format the processing results into JSON responses for presentation by the mobile application.

The Business Layer contains the TypeScript business services and Python/FastAPI machine-learning service. The TypeScript business services implement the operational rules for demand prediction, inventory management, production recommendation, POS simulation, leftover management, reporting, notifications and system administration. When prediction, confidence calculation, model training or model evaluation is required, the relevant TypeScript business service communicates with the Python/FastAPI machine-learning service through an HTTP or HTTPS REST API using JSON.

The Data Access Layer contains the TypeScript domain models and repositories, which perform the **Model** responsibilities of MVC. The domain models represent the principal system entities, while the repositories control the retrieval and storage of persistent records. Business services access stored information through these repositories instead of communicating directly with the database. This separation reduces the dependency between business logic and database-access implementation.

The Database Layer contains the Supabase PostgreSQL database. It stores user profiles, bread categories, ingredients, recipes, inventory batches, inventory movements, historical sales, prediction results, model versions, production recommendations, production decisions, simulation results, leftovers, donations, waste records, notifications, configurations and audit information. Data operations are performed through secured Supabase interfaces, while relevant database changes can produce Supabase Realtime events for delivery to the mobile application.

The server-side components also communicate with external services. OpenWeatherMap provides weather information, while Nager.Date provides public-holiday information required for prediction and POS simulation. Firebase Cloud Messaging receives eligible notification requests from the TypeScript business services and delivers background push notifications to registered mobile devices. The returned submission or delivery information is recorded where supported.

In Figure 4.1, single-direction arrows represent an internal dependency or event-delivery direction, while bidirectional arrows represent request-and-response communication between separate system components or services. The communication protocols include HTTPS REST APIs, JSON, JWT, secure Supabase interfaces and secure WebSocket connections. Sensitive service credentials are maintained within the server environment and are not exposed through the Flutter application.

This architecture enables the user interface, request controllers, business rules, machine-learning processing and database operations to be developed and maintained separately. It also ensures that the Flutter application does not communicate directly with the machine-learning service or database for protected business operations. Consequently, the architecture supports modularity, maintainability, security, controlled data access and independent component testing while remaining appropriate for a single-bakery decision-support system.

### **4.2.2 Architectural Layers and Responsibilities**  {#4.2.2-architectural-layers-and-responsibilities}

The layered architecture separates the Smart Bakery Food Waste Reduction System according to clearly defined technical responsibilities. Each layer provides specific services to the layer above it and delegates lower-level processing to the appropriate layer below it. This separation prevents the Flutter interface, request controllers, business rules and database operations from becoming tightly coupled.

Table 4.1 presents the components and responsibilities of the five principal architectural layers.

*Table 4.1: Architectural Layers and Responsibilities* 

| Architectural layer | Main components and technologies | Responsibilities |
| :---- | :---- | :---- |
| Presentation Layer | Flutter Android mobile client, screens, widgets and API client | Presents system information to the Bakery Manager and System Administrator; receives user input; provides role-based navigation; performs basic client-side validation; sends authenticated API requests; and displays loading, success, confirmation and error messages. |
| Application Layer | Node.js/Express TypeScript API controllers | Defines the backend API endpoints; receives requests from the Flutter application; validates request formats and required fields; verifies JWT authentication and role permissions; delegates valid requests to the appropriate business service; and returns structured JSON responses. |
| Business Layer | TypeScript business services and Python/FastAPI machine-learning service | Implements the main operational and decision-making rules for demand prediction, model management, inventory, production recommendation, POS simulation, leftovers, donations, waste, reporting, administration and notifications. It also performs prediction, confidence calculation, model training and model evaluation through the FastAPI service. |
| Data Access Layer | TypeScript domain models and repositories | Represents the main system entities; separates business logic from database operations; prepares database queries and updates; maps database records to domain objects; and provides controlled data-access functions to the business services. |
| Database Layer | Supabase PostgreSQL database | Stores persistent operational and historical records; maintains relationships between records; enforces database constraints; supports transaction processing; and preserves identifiers, timestamps, source classifications and audit information. |

The Presentation Layer is responsible only for interface presentation and user interaction. It does not directly perform protected database operations or invoke the Python/FastAPI machine-learning service. Instead, the Flutter API client submits authenticated requests to the TypeScript controllers through the backend API.

The Application Layer acts as the entry point to the server-side functions. Controllers determine whether a request is correctly formatted and whether the authenticated user has permission to perform the requested operation. Once the request has passed these checks, the controller delegates it to the relevant business service. Controllers do not contain the detailed algorithms for prediction, production recommendation, FIFO processing or POS simulation.

The Business Layer contains the main processing and decision rules of the proposed system. TypeScript business services coordinate the required operations and enforce the business rules established in Chapter 3\. For example, the production-recommendation service combines stored predictions, recipes and valid inventory information, while the POS simulation service validates the confirmed production decision before deducting ingredients and generating simulated sales. The Python/FastAPI service is accessed when machine-learning prediction, confidence calculation, model training or model evaluation is required.

The Data Access Layer prevents the business services from depending directly on Supabase database queries. Domain models represent entities such as bread categories, ingredients, inventory batches, predictions, production decisions and simulation results. Repositories provide controlled functions for retrieving, creating and updating the corresponding database records. This separation allows changes to the database implementation to be handled within the repository layer with fewer effects on the business logic.

The Database Layer provides persistent storage through Supabase PostgreSQL. It maintains the relationships and integrity of the stored records using primary keys, foreign keys, uniqueness rules, validation constraints and transaction support. Important multi-record operations, such as FIFO inventory deduction and POS simulation completion, are processed consistently to prevent incomplete or duplicate database updates.

Supabase Authentication, Supabase Realtime and the external services are supporting platform components rather than additional architectural layers. Their responsibilities are presented in Table 4.2.

*Table 4.2: Responsibilities of Platform and External Services*

| Supporting service | Responsibility |
| :---- | :---- |
| Supabase Authentication | Authenticates users, manages sessions, issues JWTs and supports authenticated-user retrieval. |
| Supabase Realtime | Delivers relevant database events, including in-application notification updates, to the Flutter application through a secure realtime connection. |
| OpenWeatherMap | Provides weather information required for demand prediction and POS simulation. |
| Nager.Date | Provides public-holiday information for the selected date. |
| Firebase Cloud Messaging | Accepts eligible notification requests and delivers background push notifications to registered Android devices. |

The primary processing direction is from the Presentation Layer to the Application Layer, followed by the Business Layer, Data Access Layer and Database Layer. Returned results follow the same route in the opposite direction. Supporting services are accessed only by the components that require them, as illustrated in Figure 4.1. This controlled separation improves system modularity, maintainability, security, testability and traceability. 

### **4.2.3 Application of the Model–View–Controller Pattern**  {#4.2.3-application-of-the-model–view–controller-pattern}

The Model–View–Controller pattern is incorporated within the Layered Client–Server Architecture to separate the user interface, request processing and data-management responsibilities. In the proposed system, the MVC components are distributed between the Flutter mobile client and TypeScript backend instead of operating within a single application. This distribution allows the mobile application to remain focused on user interaction while the backend controls protected operations, business processing and persistent data access.

Table 4.3 presents the implementation of each MVC component.

*Table 4.3: Application of the MVC Pattern in the Proposed System*

| MVC component | System implementation | Main responsibilities |
| :---- | :---- | :---- |
| View | Flutter screens, widgets and API client | Displays system information; provides forms, dashboards and navigation controls; receives user input; sends authenticated requests; and presents the returned results, validation messages and errors. |
| Controller | Node.js/Express TypeScript API controllers | Receives API requests from the View; validates request data; verifies authentication and role permissions; selects the appropriate business service; coordinates request processing; and returns structured JSON responses. |
| Model | TypeScript domain models and repositories | Represents system entities and their data structures; manages retrieval and persistence through repositories; maps database records to domain objects; and provides controlled access to the Supabase PostgreSQL database. |

**View**

The View is implemented using the Flutter Android mobile application. It includes the interfaces used by the Bakery Manager and System Administrator, such as login, dashboard, demand prediction, production recommendation, POS simulation, inventory management, leftover management, reporting and notification screens.

The View displays information received from the backend and captures user actions. It may perform basic interface validation, such as checking whether a required field is empty, but it does not determine production feasibility, calculate prediction results, perform FIFO deduction or directly modify protected database records. These responsibilities are delegated to server-side components.

**Controller**

The Controller is implemented using TypeScript API controllers within the Node.js/Express backend. Each controller provides an entry point for a related group of system operations. For example, a prediction controller receives demand-prediction requests, while an inventory controller receives ingredient, recipe and inventory-management requests.

Before processing a protected request, the controller verifies the JWT and identifies the authenticated user. It then checks whether the user’s role permits the requested operation and validates the supplied request information. A valid request is delegated to the appropriate TypeScript business service. After processing is completed, the controller returns a structured response containing the result, status and relevant message to the Flutter View.

Controllers coordinate requests but do not contain the complete operational logic. This prevents controllers from becoming excessively large and allows the business rules to be tested separately from the API endpoints.

**Model**

The Model responsibilities are implemented through TypeScript domain models and repositories. Domain models represent important system entities, including users, bread categories, ingredients, recipes, inventory batches, predictions, model versions, production recommendations, production decisions, simulations, leftovers, donations, waste records and notifications.

Repositories provide controlled database-access operations for these models. They retrieve, create and update records in the Supabase PostgreSQL database and return the results to the business services. The View and controllers do not directly execute database queries.

**Supporting Business and Machine-Learning Services**

The proposed implementation extends the traditional MVC pattern with a Business-Service Layer and a specialized Machine-Learning Service. These services are not separate MVC elements; they support the Controller and Model by isolating complex processing from request handling and data access.

TypeScript business services implement the operational rules defined in Chapter 3\. The Python/FastAPI machine-learning service performs feature preparation, Random Forest prediction, Linear Regression comparison, confidence calculation, model training and model evaluation. The TypeScript business services communicate with the FastAPI service and use the Model and repositories to retrieve required data and store processing results.

For example, when the Bakery Manager generates a next-day demand prediction:

1. The Flutter View submits the prediction request to the TypeScript Controller.  
2. The Controller verifies the user, role and request information.  
3. The Controller delegates the request to the prediction business service.  
4. The business service retrieves the required historical and contextual data through the Model and repositories.  
5. The business service sends the prepared request to the Python/FastAPI machine-learning service.  
6. The machine-learning service returns the prediction, confidence indicator and supporting information.  
7. The business service stores the generated result through the repository.  
8. The Controller returns the result to the Flutter View.  
9. The View presents the generated prediction to the Bakery Manager.

This implementation maintains the separation among presentation, request control, business processing and persistent data management. Consequently, changes to the Flutter interfaces, backend controllers, machine-learning algorithms or database operations can be implemented with fewer effects on the other system components.

### **4.2.4 Communication Protocols and Component Interactions** {#4.2.4-communication-protocols-and-component-interactions}

The components of the Smart Bakery Food Waste Reduction System communicate through secured network protocols and controlled internal interfaces. The mobile application, backend services, machine-learning service, database platform and external services exchange information using standardized formats to support interoperability and consistent error handling.

Most network communication follows a synchronous request-and-response approach. The requesting component sends a request and waits for a success result or error response. Supabase Realtime and Firebase Cloud Messaging use asynchronous communication because they can deliver notification events to the Flutter application without requiring the user to submit a new request.

Table 4.4 presents the communication mechanisms used by the proposed system.

*Table 4.4: Communication Protocols and Component Interactions* 

| Communicating components | Protocol or mechanism | Data format or security | Purpose |
| :---- | :---- | :---- | :---- |
| Flutter application ↔ Supabase Authentication | HTTPS through the Supabase Authentication API | Credentials, JWT and authenticated-user information | Authenticates users, issues tokens, manages sessions and supports secure logout. |
| Flutter application ↔ TypeScript API Controller | HTTPS REST API | JSON, JWT and TLS 1.2 or later | Submits authenticated functional requests and receives structured results from the backend. |
| TypeScript API Controller ↔ Supabase Authentication | HTTPS through the Supabase Authentication API | JWT validation and authenticated-user information | Validates the supplied token and retrieves the authenticated user where required. |
| TypeScript Controller → TypeScript Business Service | In-process TypeScript method call | Typed parameters and returned objects | Delegates validated requests to the appropriate business operation. |
| TypeScript Business Service → Model and Repository | In-process TypeScript method call | Domain objects and typed parameters | Retrieves or stores persistent information without placing database operations directly in the business logic. |
| TypeScript Business Service ↔ Python/FastAPI Service | HTTP or HTTPS REST API | JSON request and response | Requests demand prediction, confidence calculation, model training and model evaluation. |
| Repository ↔ Supabase PostgreSQL | Secured Supabase API over HTTPS | Database records, JSON and TLS | Retrieves, creates, updates and validates persistent system records. |
| TypeScript Business Service ↔ OpenWeatherMap | HTTPS REST API | JSON | Retrieves weather information required for prediction and POS simulation. |
| TypeScript Business Service ↔ Nager.Date | HTTPS REST API | JSON | Retrieves public-holiday information for the selected date. |
| TypeScript Business Service ↔ Firebase Cloud Messaging | HTTPS service request | JSON, device token and secured server credentials | Submits eligible background notifications and receives a submission result. |
| Supabase PostgreSQL → Supabase Realtime → Flutter application | Secure WebSocket connection | Realtime event payload using WSS | Delivers relevant in-application notification updates. |
| Firebase Cloud Messaging → Flutter application | Firebase push-notification channel | Push-notification payload | Delivers background notifications to a registered Android device. |

The Flutter application communicates with the TypeScript backend through REST API endpoints. Protected requests include the JWT issued by Supabase Authentication in the request authorisation information. JSON is used as the primary data-interchange format because it is supported by Flutter, Express, FastAPI, Supabase and the selected external services.

The backend API uses standard HTTP operations according to the requested action. Retrieval operations use GET, record-creation or processing operations use POST, updates use PUT or PATCH, and supported removal operations use DELETE. The backend returns appropriate HTTP status codes together with a structured JSON response. Successful processing may return status codes such as 200 OK or 201 Created, while invalid, unauthenticated or unauthorised requests return suitable client-error responses. Server or external-service failures return an error response without exposing sensitive implementation information.

The TypeScript Controller, Business Service, and Model and Repository components operate within the same Node.js/Express backend process. Therefore, they communicate through internal TypeScript method calls rather than HTTP requests. The Controller calls a business service after authentication and validation, while the business service calls a repository when persistent information is required. Return values follow the same internal call path in the opposite direction.

The Python/FastAPI machine-learning service operates as a separate server process. During local development, the Express backend and FastAPI service may run on the same computer using different port numbers and communicate through a local HTTP REST endpoint. In the deployed environment, the communication should use HTTPS or an otherwise protected internal connection. The FastAPI service is accessible through the TypeScript backend and is not invoked directly by the Flutter application.

OpenWeatherMap and Nager.Date are accessed through HTTPS only when contextual information is required for a manually initiated prediction or POS simulation. If an external service is temporarily unavailable, the TypeScript backend returns an understandable error or applies the approved available-data handling rule. External-service credentials are stored in the server environment and are not included in the Flutter source code or APK.

Notification communication follows two approaches. Supabase Realtime delivers in-application notification events through a secure WebSocket connection when the application is active. Firebase Cloud Messaging delivers eligible background push notifications using the registered device token when the application is not active. The system checks the user’s notification preference and device-token validity before submitting a background notification and records the submission or delivery status where supported.

Single-direction arrows in Figure 4.1 represent internal dependencies or event-delivery direction. Bidirectional arrows represent request-and-response communication between separate components or services. All major prediction, model-retraining, production-decision and POS-simulation operations remain manually initiated by authorised users and are not triggered automatically through these communication mechanisms.

## **4.3 System Design Strategies** {#4.3-system-design-strategies}

This chapter selects a combination of **Modular Design, Object-Oriented Design and Component-Based Software Engineering principles** for the Smart Bakery Food Waste Reduction System. These strategies address different aspects of the system design and are applied together rather than treated as mutually exclusive alternatives.

Modular Design is selected as the primary strategy because the proposed system consists of multiple functional areas with clearly defined responsibilities. Object-Oriented Design supports the internal implementation of these modules through domain models, controllers, services and repositories. Component-based principles support the integration of the Flutter application, Express backend, FastAPI machine-learning service, Supabase platform and external APIs through defined interfaces.

*Table 4.5: Selected Design Strategies of the Proposed System* 

| Design strategy | Role in the system | Application |
| :---- | :---- | :---- |
| Modular Design | Primary design strategy | Separates the system into eight functional modules with controlled responsibilities and dependencies. |
| Object-Oriented Design | Internal implementation strategy | Represents system entities and behaviours using classes, objects, attributes and methods in Dart, TypeScript and Python. |
| Component-Based principles | Supporting integration strategy | Enables independently operating services, platforms and external APIs to communicate through defined interfaces and data formats. |

The following subsections describe the application of each strategy and explain how they collectively support the proposed system’s maintainability, modularity, testability and integration requirements. 

### **4.3.1 Modular Design** {#4.3.1-modular-design}

Modular Design divides a system into separate functional areas, with each module responsible for a related group of operations. It is selected as the primary design strategy for the Smart Bakery Food Waste Reduction System because the system contains several interconnected but distinguishable bakery-management functions.

The proposed system is divided into eight functional modules:

1. User and Access Management  
2. Demand Prediction  
3. Inventory and Smart Production Recommendation  
4. POS and Sales Simulation  
5. Leftover, Donation and Waste Management  
6. Reporting and Dashboard  
7. Alerts and Notifications  
8. System Administration

Each module contains the controllers, services, domain models and repositories required to perform its responsibilities. The modules exchange information through controlled service interfaces and shared domain structures instead of directly accessing the internal implementation of another module.

Table 4.6 summarises the responsibility and principal interactions of each module.

*Table 4.6: Responsibilities and Interactions of the Functional Modules*

| Functional module | Primary responsibility | Principal interactions |
| :---- | :---- | :---- |
| User and Access Management | Manages login, logout, profiles, user accounts, roles and access permissions. | Uses Supabase Authentication and provides authenticated-user and role information to protected modules. |
| Demand Prediction | Prepares prediction features, generates next-day predictions, calculates confidence, manages model training and evaluates model versions. | Uses historical sales, weather and holiday information; provides predictions to the Production Recommendation, Reporting and Notification modules. |
| Inventory and Smart Production Recommendation | Manages ingredients, bread categories, recipes, inventory batches, FIFO processing, production feasibility, recommendations and confirmed decisions. | Uses predictions and configured parameters; provides confirmed production decisions to POS Simulation and inventory information to Reporting and Notifications. |
| POS and Sales Simulation | Simulates bakery sales using a stored prediction and confirmed production decision; records units sold, lost sales, revenue and leftovers. | Uses production decisions, inventory, weather and holiday information; provides results to Leftover Management, Reporting and Notifications. |
| Leftover, Donation and Waste Management | Records calculated leftovers and manages their allocation to donation, waste or unallocated quantities. | Uses completed simulation results and charity-partner records; provides donation and waste information to Reporting and Notifications. |
| Reporting and Dashboard | Aggregates operational and simulation records into dashboards, indicators and supported report exports. | Retrieves information from prediction, inventory, production, simulation, leftover, donation and waste records without modifying the original records. |
| Alerts and Notifications | Generates and presents low-stock, low-confidence, lost-sales, leftover, donation and system-failure notifications. | Receives relevant events from other modules and uses Supabase Realtime or Firebase Cloud Messaging for delivery. |
| System Administration | Manages bakery settings, system parameters, external-service configurations and audit information. | Provides configurable values to prediction, inventory, simulation and notification functions. |

The modules are designed with controlled dependencies. The Demand Prediction module produces prediction results but does not determine the final production quantity. Instead, the Inventory and Smart Production Recommendation module combines the stored prediction with recipes and valid inventory information to produce a feasible recommendation. The Bakery Manager then confirms the final production decision before it becomes available to the POS Simulation module.

The POS Simulation module uses the confirmed production decision and stored prediction for the selected date. Before simulated sales processing begins, it validates and deducts the required ingredients through FIFO inventory operations. The resulting sales, lost-sales and leftover records are subsequently made available to the Leftover, Donation and Waste Management module and Reporting and Dashboard module.

The Reporting and Dashboard module primarily performs read and aggregation operations. It does not modify the original prediction, inventory, production, simulation or leftover records used to generate a report. Similarly, the Alerts and Notifications module reacts to relevant events produced by other modules but does not automatically initiate predictions, model retraining, production confirmation or POS simulation.

This modular separation supports the tailored Agile development process because individual modules can be implemented and tested incrementally before complete system integration. Changes within one module can also be managed with fewer effects on unrelated functions, provided that its shared interfaces and data structures remain consistent. The detailed organization and dependencies of these modules are subsequently represented in the Development View of the Four-Plus-One Architectural View Model.

### **4.3.2 Object-Oriented Design** {#4.3.2-object-oriented-design}

Object-Oriented Design is selected to support the internal implementation of the functional modules. It organizes software around classes and objects that combine related data and behaviours. This approach is suitable because the proposed system contains many identifiable entities, including users, bread categories, ingredients, inventory batches, predictions, production decisions, simulations, leftovers, donations and notifications.

The technologies selected for the system support object-oriented implementation. Dart is an object-oriented language used to implement the Flutter mobile application. TypeScript supports classes, interfaces, access modifiers, inheritance and object composition for the Express backend. Python also supports classes and objects for organizing feature preparation, prediction, model training and evaluation functions in the FastAPI machine-learning service.

The application of the principal object-oriented concepts is presented in Table 4.7.

*Table 4.7: Application of Object-Oriented Design Principles*

| Object-oriented principle | Application in the proposed system |
| :---- | :---- |
| Encapsulation | Related data and operations are grouped within classes. Internal data is accessed through controlled methods instead of being modified directly by unrelated components. |
| Abstraction | Controllers, services and repositories expose only the operations required by other components while hiding their internal processing and database-access details. |
| Composition | Controllers use business services, business services use repositories, and services use external-service adapters. This is preferred for combining responsibilities without creating unnecessary inheritance relationships. |
| Inheritance | Shared behaviour may be placed in a base class where several classes require genuinely common functions, such as common error or model-processing behaviour. |
| Separation of responsibility | Each class is assigned a focused responsibility, such as request handling, business processing, data access or entity representation. |

**Class Organization**

The proposed classes are grouped according to their architectural responsibilities. Table 4.8 presents the main class categories and representative examples.

*Table 4.8: Main Object-Oriented Class Categories* 

| Class category | Representative classes | Responsibility |
| ----- | ----- | ----- |
| Flutter View classes | LoginScreen, DashboardScreen, PredictionScreen, ProductionRecommendationScreen, PosSimulationScreen | Present information, receive user input and manage screen-level interaction. |
| API Controller classes | AuthController, PredictionController, InventoryController, PosSimulationController, ReportController | Receive and validate API requests, verify permissions and delegate valid operations to business services. |
| Business-Service classes | PredictionOrchestrationService, InventoryService, RecommendationEngine, PosSimulationService, LeftoverManagementService, ReportService, NotificationService | Implement business rules and coordinate operations involving models, repositories and external services. |
| Domain Model classes | BreadCategory, Ingredient, Recipe, InventoryBatch, DailyPrediction, ProductionDecision, DailyProduction, SalesTransaction, DailyResult, WasteRecord, Donation | Represent the principal business entities and their relevant attributes. |
| Repository classes | DailyPredictionRepo, InventoryBatchRepo, ProductionDecisionRepo, DailyResultRepo, DonationRepo, NotificationRepo | Provide controlled data-retrieval and persistence operations for the domain models. |
| External-Service Adapter classes | WeatherService, HolidayService, PushNotificationService | Encapsulate communication with OpenWeatherMap, Nager.Date and Firebase Cloud Messaging. |
| Machine-Learning classes | FeaturePreparationService, PredictionService, ModelTrainingService, ModelEvaluationService | Prepare features, generate predictions, calculate confidence, train models and evaluate model performance. |

The class names in Table 4.8 represent the planned logical responsibilities. 

**Encapsulation of Business Operations**

Encapsulation is applied to prevent system records from being modified through uncontrolled operations. For example, an inventory quantity is not changed directly by the Flutter interface. The interface submits a request to the Inventory Controller, which delegates the operation to the Inventory Service. The service validates the operation and uses the Inventory Repository to update the relevant inventory batches and movement records.

Similarly, production recommendations are calculated by the backend rather than directly by the mobile application. The RecommendationEngine retrieves the required prediction, recipe and inventory data through the appropriate repositories, calculates production feasibility and returns the recommendations for review. When the Bakery Manager confirms a production decision, the ProductionDecisionService revalidates feasibility and uses the ProductionDecisionRepo to store the recommendation snapshot together with the confirmed quantity, decision type, reason and manager information. Confirming the decision does not deduct ingredient inventory.

This controlled processing path can be represented as:

View→Controller→Service→Repository→Database

**Abstraction through Public Operations and Adapter Boundaries**

Abstraction is achieved through focused public operations and specialised adapter classes rather than through separate service or repository interface classifiers. Controllers, business services and repositories expose only the operations required by their dependent classes while hiding their internal processing, database queries and provider-specific implementation details.

External-service adapter classes provide boundaries between the business logic and external providers. For example, OpenWeatherMapClient exposes an operation for retrieving weather information for a specified date and location. The ContextService uses this public operation without depending on the provider-specific request format or response structure used by OpenWeatherMap.

The same abstraction approach is applied through:

* NagerDateClient for calendar and public-holiday retrieval;  
* the notification adapter or gateway for Firebase Cloud Messaging submission;  
* FastApiMlClient for prediction, training and evaluation requests to the Python/FastAPI service;  
* repository classes for controlled Supabase PostgreSQL operations; and  
* ReportExportAdapter for generating PDF and CSV report outputs.

Each adapter converts provider-specific data and errors into structures understood by the system. Consequently, the business services remain independent of the internal implementation details of Supabase, OpenWeatherMap, Nager.Date, Firebase Cloud Messaging and FastAPI. This design reduces coupling and allows an adapter implementation to be modified or replaced with fewer changes to the business logic.

**Composition and Controlled Dependencies**

Object composition is preferred when one class requires the functionality of another. A Controller contains or receives a reference to the required Business Service, while the Business Service receives references to its repositories and external-service adapters. For example, the Prediction Service may use a Prediction Repository, Historical Sales Repository, Weather Service, Holiday Service and Machine-Learning Service.

This approach avoids placing unrelated responsibilities into one large class. It also supports unit testing because a required dependency can be replaced with a controlled test implementation when the class is tested independently.

**Application across Different Languages**

The Flutter application, TypeScript backend and Python/FastAPI service operate in separate runtime environments. Therefore, they do not share the same in-memory class objects. Instead, equivalent request and response structures are exchanged using JSON. Each component converts the received data into its own language-specific model or data-transfer object.

For example, a prediction request produced by the TypeScript service is converted into JSON and sent to the FastAPI service. Python validates the received structure, processes the prediction and returns a JSON response. The TypeScript backend then converts the response into its own prediction result model before storing it and returning the relevant information to Flutter.

Object-Oriented Design therefore provides a consistent method for organizing the internal code of each system component. It improves clarity, maintainability, reuse and testability by assigning focused responsibilities to classes and controlling the dependencies among the presentation, controller, business-service, machine-learning and data-access components. The main classes and their relationships are subsequently presented in the Logical View of the Four-Plus-One Architectural View Model.

### **4.3.3 Application of Component-Based Principles** {#4.3.3-application-of-component-based-principles}

Component-Based Software Engineering principles are applied as a supporting design strategy for integrating the major client, server, platform and external-service components of the Smart Bakery Food Waste Reduction System. The system does not adopt complete Component-Based Software Engineering as its primary strategy. Instead, it applies principles such as component independence, defined interfaces, low coupling, replaceability and controlled dependencies.

A software component provides a specific set of functions through a defined interface without requiring other components to understand its internal implementation. This principle is particularly suitable for the proposed system because the Flutter application, Express backend, FastAPI machine-learning service, Supabase platform and external services operate as separate components that use different technologies.

Table 4.9 presents the principal components and their interfaces.

*Table 4.9: Principal Software Components and Interfaces*

| Component | Provided interface | Required components or services | Primary responsibility |
| :---- | :---- | :---- | :---- |
| Flutter Android Mobile Client | User interfaces and mobile interaction | Express REST API, Supabase Authentication, Supabase Realtime and Firebase Cloud Messaging | Provides screens, navigation and user interaction for the Bakery Manager and System Administrator. |
| Node.js/Express TypeScript Backend | HTTPS REST API using JSON | Supabase services, FastAPI machine-learning service and external APIs | Processes authenticated requests, applies business rules and coordinates system operations. |
| Python/FastAPI Machine-Learning Service | Prediction, training and evaluation REST endpoints | Validated data supplied by the TypeScript backend | Performs feature preparation, demand prediction, confidence calculation, model training and model evaluation. |
| Supabase Authentication | Authentication and user-management API | User credentials and JWT requests | Authenticates users, issues tokens, manages sessions and provides authenticated-user information. |
| Supabase PostgreSQL Database | Secured Supabase database interface | Repository requests from the TypeScript backend | Stores operational, historical, configuration and audit records. |
| Supabase Realtime | Secure realtime event channel | Relevant PostgreSQL record changes | Delivers in-application notification events to the Flutter application. |
| OpenWeatherMap Adapter | Weather-retrieval interface | OpenWeatherMap HTTPS API | Retrieves and converts weather information into the format required by the business services. |
| Nager.Date Adapter | Public-holiday retrieval interface | Nager.Date HTTPS API | Retrieves and converts public-holiday information for a selected date. |
| Firebase Cloud Messaging Adapter | Background-notification submission interface | Firebase Cloud Messaging service | Submits eligible background notifications and processes returned delivery information where supported. |

**Defined Component Interfaces**

Each component exposes only the operations required by other components. The Flutter application accesses protected system operations through the Express REST API rather than directly accessing the FastAPI service or protected database operations. Similarly, the TypeScript business services access database records through repositories rather than embedding Supabase queries throughout the business logic.

The FastAPI service exposes machine-learning operations through defined API endpoints. A prediction request contains the validated features and required prediction information, while the response contains the generated prediction, confidence indicator, model version and supporting information. The TypeScript backend does not need to understand how Random Forest processes its decision trees internally.

A component interface should define:

* The operation or endpoint name  
* Required input fields  
* Input data types  
* Response structure  
* Possible error responses  
* Authentication requirements  
* Communication protocol and data format

Defined interfaces reduce ambiguity and help ensure that independently developed components exchange compatible information.

**Low Coupling**

Low coupling means that a component depends on another component’s interface rather than its internal implementation. For example, the TypeScript backend depends on the FastAPI prediction endpoint, but it does not directly depend on the internal Python classes used to load and execute the Random Forest model.

External-service adapters also reduce coupling between the business logic and external providers. The business services request weather, holiday or notification operations through an internal service interface. The adapter is responsible for constructing the provider-specific request and converting the returned response into a system-defined format.

The interaction can be represented as:

Business Service→Service Interface→External-Service Adapter→External API

This prevents provider-specific request formats from being distributed throughout the business layer.

**Component Replaceability**

Clearly defined interfaces allow a component implementation to be modified or replaced with fewer effects on the complete system. For example, a weather-service provider could be replaced in the future if the new adapter provides the same system-defined weather information. The production and prediction business rules would not require major changes because they depend on the internal weather-service interface rather than directly depending on OpenWeatherMap.

The same principle applies to:

* Replacing or modifying a holiday-data provider  
* Updating the Firebase notification adapter  
* Modifying the FastAPI machine-learning implementation  
* Changing repository queries or Supabase data-access operations  
* Updating Flutter interfaces without changing backend business rules

Replaceability does not mean that a component can be changed without testing. The replacement must still satisfy the defined interface and data requirements, and integration testing must verify that the components continue to communicate correctly.

**Independent Development and Testing**

Component boundaries allow the major parts of the system to be tested independently. The Express backend can be tested using controlled responses that represent the FastAPI service, while the FastAPI prediction endpoints can be tested using prepared JSON requests without running the Flutter application. External-service adapters can also be tested using controlled API responses for successful, invalid and unavailable-service conditions.

This separation supports the tailored Agile methodology because components can be implemented and integrated incrementally. For example, the production-recommendation business logic can initially use a prepared prediction response before it is integrated with the completed FastAPI service.

**Failure Isolation**

Component-based principles also support failure isolation. If OpenWeatherMap or Nager.Date is temporarily unavailable, the failure is handled by the relevant adapter and business service rather than causing unrelated functions such as inventory viewing or profile management to fail. Similarly, failure during FastAPI model training does not automatically replace or invalidate the current active model.

Component failures are converted into structured error responses or notification events. This enables the Flutter application to present understandable messages and, where appropriate, provide a retry option without exposing internal service details.

The application of component-based principles therefore supports the integration of technologies with different programming languages, runtime environments and communication mechanisms. It complements Modular Design by defining the technical components that support the functional modules and complements Object-Oriented Design by using service, adapter and repository interfaces within those components. The arrangement and dependencies of the components are subsequently presented in the Development View of the Four-Plus-One Architectural View Model.

### **4.3.4 Combined Application and Justification** {#4.3.4-combined-application-and-justification}

Modular Design, Object-Oriented Design and Component-Based principles are applied together because each strategy addresses a different aspect of the Smart Bakery Food Waste Reduction System. No single strategy sufficiently defines the functional organization, internal software structure and integration requirements of the complete system.

Modular Design provides the overall functional separation of the system. Object-Oriented Design structures the internal implementation of each module using classes and objects. Component-based principles define how independently operating client, server, platform and external-service components communicate through controlled interfaces.

The relationship among the selected strategies is presented in Table 4.10.

*Table 4.10: Combined Application of the Selected Design Strategies*

| Design concern | Applied strategy | Resulting design |
| :---- | :---- | :---- |
| Separation of bakery functions | Modular Design | The system is divided into eight functional modules with clearly defined responsibilities. |
| Internal code organization | Object-Oriented Design | Controllers, services, models, repositories and adapters are represented using focused classes and interfaces. |
| Client and server separation | Component-Based principles | Flutter, Express and FastAPI operate as separate components connected through REST APIs. |
| External-service integration | Component-Based principles and Object-Oriented Design | Weather, holiday and notification providers are accessed through adapter and service interfaces. |
| Data-access separation | Object-Oriented Design | Repository classes isolate Supabase operations from controllers and business services. |
| Incremental development | Modular Design and Component-Based principles | Modules and technical components can be implemented, tested and integrated progressively. |
| Maintainability | All three strategies | Changes can be concentrated within the affected module, class or service component. |
| Testability | All three strategies | Modules, classes, API endpoints, repositories and external-service adapters can be tested independently. |

**Application to a System Operation**

The combined application of the strategies can be demonstrated through the next-day demand-prediction operation.

At the modular level, the operation belongs to the Demand Prediction module. Other modules do not directly implement or duplicate its prediction responsibilities. The Inventory and Smart Production Recommendation module subsequently uses the stored prediction output through a controlled system interface.

Within the Demand Prediction module, Object-Oriented Design separates the operation into focused classes. The PredictionController receives and validates the request, the PredictionService coordinates the operation, and the required repositories retrieve historical sales and store the generated result. Machine-learning-related classes prepare the features, execute the model and calculate the prediction confidence.

Component-based principles support communication with the independently operating services. The TypeScript Prediction Service obtains contextual data through weather and holiday adapters and sends the prepared prediction request to the Python/FastAPI machine-learning component through a defined REST API. The internal Python implementation remains hidden from the TypeScript backend.

The combined interaction can therefore be represented as:

![][image11]

This example demonstrates that the strategies are applied at different levels rather than performing the same function.

**Design Rules Resulting from the Combined Strategy**

The following rules guide the implementation of the combined design:

1. Each functional responsibility shall be assigned to an appropriate module.  
2. A module shall not directly modify records owned by another module without using an approved service or repository operation.  
3. Flutter Views shall communicate with protected business operations through TypeScript API Controllers.  
4. Controllers shall delegate complex processing to Business Services.  
5. Business Services shall access persistent records through repositories.  
6. The Flutter application shall not directly invoke the FastAPI machine-learning service.  
7. External APIs shall be accessed through service or adapter interfaces.  
8. Component-specific credentials and implementation details shall remain hidden from unrelated components.  
9. Cross-module data structures and API request formats shall be defined consistently.  
10. Prediction, model retraining, production confirmation and POS simulation shall remain manually initiated by authorised users.

These rules reduce direct dependency among the user interface, business logic, database and external services. They also prevent the duplication of system rules across multiple components.

**Justification for the Combined Selection**

Modular Design alone would separate the system into functional areas but would not sufficiently define the internal classes or the interfaces used to integrate different technologies. Object-Oriented Design alone would organize classes and objects but would not clearly describe the functional modules or independently operating services. Using complete Component-Based Software Engineering as the sole strategy could introduce unnecessary component and interface complexity for a single-developer FYP.

Therefore, Modular Design is selected as the primary strategy, while Object-Oriented Design and Component-Based principles provide supporting structures. This combination is appropriate because the system contains multiple related bakery functions, uses three programming languages or environments, and integrates machine-learning, database and external-service components.

The combined design supports:

* Clear separation of functional and technical responsibilities  
* Incremental Agile development  
* Independent module and component testing  
* Controlled API and database access  
* Replacement or modification of external-service implementations  
* Maintenance of business rules without direct dependency on the user interface  
* Integration of Flutter, TypeScript, Python and Supabase technologies

The selected design strategies establish the structural foundation for the proposed system. Their application is subsequently represented from logical, process, development, physical and scenario perspectives through the Four-Plus-One Architectural View Model in Section 4.4.

## **4.4 Four-Plus-One Architectural View Model**  {#4.4-four-plus-one-architectural-view-model}

The Four-Plus-One Architectural View Model is applied to present the design of the Smart Bakery Food Waste Reduction System from multiple complementary perspectives. The architecture diagram in Section 4.2 presents the overall system structure, while the Four-Plus-One View Model provides more detailed representations of the system’s object structure, runtime processes, software organization, deployment environment and user scenarios.

The model consists of four principal views: the Logical View, Process View, Development View and Physical View. These views are supported by the Scenario View, which represents the “plus one” view. The Scenario View connects the architectural design to the use cases and requirements established in Chapter 3\.

The five views are not separate system architectures. They represent the same proposed system from different perspectives. Together, they provide a more complete explanation than a single architecture or design diagram.

### **4.4.1 Overview of the Four-Plus-One View Model**  {#4.4.1-overview-of-the-four-plus-one-view-model}

Figure 4.2 presents the application of the Four-Plus-One View Model to the proposed system.![][image12]

*Figure 4.2: Four-Plus-One Architectural View Model of the Proposed System*

The Scenario View is positioned at the centre because the use cases provide the functional scenarios that guide and validate the other architectural views. For example, the Generate Demand Prediction scenario requires suitable classes in the Logical View, processing interactions in the Process View, software components in the Development View and deployment nodes in the Physical View.

Table 4.11 summarises the purpose and design artefacts of each view.

*Table 4.11: Application of the Four-Plus-One Architectural Views*

| Architectural view | Main design concern | Application in the proposed system | Design artefact |
| :---- | :---- | :---- | :---- |
| Logical View | Static object-oriented structure | Represents the principal domain entities, controllers, services and repositories together with their relationships. | Class diagram |
| Process View | Runtime behaviour and interaction | Describes the sequence of activities, decisions and component interactions involved in major workflows. | Activity diagrams  |
| Development View | Software organization | Shows the eight functional modules and the technical components used to implement them. | Component diagram |
| Physical View | Deployment environment | Shows the Android client, Express backend, FastAPI machine-learning service, Supabase platform and external services. | Deployment diagram |
| Scenario View (+1) | User and system requirements | Demonstrates how the architecture supports the Bakery Manager, System Administrator and supporting external-service interactions. | Use case diagrams established in Chapter 3 |

The **Logical View** focuses on the object-oriented structure of the system. It identifies classes representing system entities and processing responsibilities, including controllers, business services, domain models and repositories. Their attributes, operations and relationships are represented using a class diagram.

The **Process View** focuses on system behaviour during operation. Activity diagrams describe the runtime flow, decisions and responsibilities involved in the system’s major operational processes. 

The **Development View** focuses on the organization of the software implementation. It shows how the eight functional modules are divided and how they depend on shared technical components such as authentication, database access, machine learning, external-data adapters and notification delivery.

The **Physical View** focuses on the deployment of the system components. It identifies the Android device, server-side processes, Supabase cloud platform and external services together with the network connections used among them. The Express backend and FastAPI machine-learning service may operate as separate processes using different ports, even when hosted on the same physical server.

The **Scenario View** represents the actors and use cases established in Chapter 3\. The Bakery Manager and System Administrator interact with the system according to their assigned responsibilities, while the Weather Service, Calendar/Holiday Service and Push Notification Service support specific system operations. Instead of repeating the complete use case specifications, the Scenario View relates the existing use cases to the architectural components that implement them.

### **4.4.2 Logical View** {#4.4.2-logical-view}

The Logical View presents the static object-oriented structure of the Core Application. It is represented through one overview class diagram supported by detailed diagrams showing the principal Controller-to-Service, Service-to-Repository and Repository-to-Domain Model relationships. The diagrams focus on the architecturally important classes and dependencies required to implement the main system responsibilities.

The Logical View applies the Object-Oriented Design strategy described in Section 4.3.2. Encapsulation is achieved by assigning focused responsibilities to presentation boundaries, controllers, business services, repositories, adapters and domain models. Flutter View classes present information and receive user input, while the API Client encapsulates communication with the TypeScript backend. Controllers validate application requests and delegate processing, business services implement and coordinate system rules, repositories isolate Supabase PostgreSQL operations, and adapters encapsulate communication with external services.

The design follows the dependency direction established by the layered MVC architecture:

* Flutter View → API Client → TypeScript Controller;  
* TypeScript Controller → Business Service;  
* Business Service → Repository or External-Service Adapter;  
* Repository → Supabase PostgreSQL; and  
* TypeScript Machine-Learning Client → FastAPI Machine-Learning API.

Dependencies flow towards the components that provide the required operation. Returned data follow the corresponding request path in the opposite direction, but this does not reverse the structural dependency between the classes.

Node.js and Express are responsible for application orchestration and database access. Only the TypeScript repositories communicate with Supabase PostgreSQL. The Python/FastAPI machine-learning service receives validated prediction, training and evaluation data from the TypeScript backend and returns calculated results without directly accessing the application database.

The present Logical View focuses on the Core Application. The Python/FastAPI machine-learning service is represented as a subsystem boundary because its internal classes are independently organised. A separate detailed machine-learning class diagram may be added during implementation if required.

The class relationships use associations for stable relationships between domain entities, composition where an object owns contained data, and dependencies where one class uses another to perform its responsibility. Repository inheritance is represented only where concrete repositories extend the proposed `BaseRepo<T>` parent class. Interface realisation is not shown because the current proposed design does not define separate service or repository interfaces. 

To maintain readability, the Logical View is presented using one overview and three detailed class diagrams. Figure 4.3(a) summarises the dependency direction among the principal software packages. Figure 4.3(b) presents the relationships between TypeScript controllers and business services. Figure 4.3(c) presents the dependencies among business services, repositories and external-service adapters, including repository inheritance. Figure 4.3(d) presents the core domain models together with their associations, multiplicities, aggregation and composition relationship.

*![][image14]*

*![][image15]*
