### **4.6.4 Interaction, Validation and Feedback Design** {#4.6.4-interaction,-validation-and-feedback-design}

The user interface is designed to provide immediate feedback and prevent invalid operations before data is submitted to the backend. Validation is applied at both the input and business-rule levels. Input validation checks required fields, date formats, numerical values and permitted ranges, while business-rule validation checks whether an operation is feasible according to the current system data.

Table 4.24 summarises the principal validation and feedback mechanisms.

*Table 4.24: User-Interface Validation and Feedback Design*

| Interaction area | Validation or feedback | Interface response |
| :---- | :---- | :---- |
| Login | Email address and password are required. | Invalid or missing information is displayed near the affected field without clearing the entered email address. |
| Demand prediction | A valid future target date must be selected. | The Generate button remains unavailable until a valid date is provided. Progress feedback is shown while contextual data and predictions are being retrieved. |
| Prediction confidence | Model confidence is compared with the configured 75% threshold. | A low-confidence warning advises the manager to review the prediction before confirming production. Cold-start results are separately identified as heuristic estimates. |
| Production decision | The selected quantity must be non-negative and must not exceed the maximum producible quantity. | Invalid recommendations cannot be accepted, and the interface requests an adjusted feasible quantity. |
| POS simulation | A confirmed production decision and sufficient ingredient quantities must be available. | Simulation is prevented when a prerequisite fails, and the reason is displayed. The action button is disabled while processing to avoid duplicate submissions. |
| Leftover allocation | Donation or waste quantity must not exceed the remaining unallocated leftovers. | The Record Allocation button remains disabled until a valid action and quantity are entered. |
| Model training | Sufficient validated historical records must be available. | Training is prevented when the dataset is insufficient, and the administrator is informed of the required corrective action. |
| Model activation | A candidate model must have completed evaluation before activation. | Evaluation results are presented for review, and explicit administrator confirmation is required before activation. |
| System settings | Values must conform to their permitted type and range. | Invalid values are rejected while the previous valid setting is retained. |
| External services | Weather, holiday or notification services may be unavailable. | The interface displays service status and an understandable failure message without exposing technical credentials or internal error details. |

Consistent visual feedback is used throughout the application. Green indicates successful or completed operations, amber indicates warnings or conditions requiring review, red indicates errors or blocked operations, and blue presents informational guidance. Colour is supported by icons and explanatory text so that users do not need to depend on colour alone to understand the message.

Potentially important actions require explicit confirmation. These include confirming a production decision, recording leftover allocation and activating a candidate prediction model. If validation fails, the user’s valid input is preserved so that only the incorrect value needs to be corrected. Previous valid information, such as the active model version and system settings, is retained when an attempted update fails.

Action buttons display disabled, processing, success or failure states according to the current interaction. Duplicate submissions are prevented while an operation is being processed. These mechanisms support user guidance, recoverability, consistency and minimal surprise by clearly communicating what occurred, why an action cannot continue and what the user should do next.

## **4.7 Report Design** {#4.7-report-design}

### **4.7.1 Report Design Overview** {#4.7.1-report-design-overview}

The reporting design transforms stored operational data into summaries that support production planning, waste monitoring and bakery performance evaluation. Reports are generated on demand by the Bakery Manager or System Administrator rather than through an automatic reporting schedule. The Reporting and Dashboard module requests the selected reporting period and bread-category filter through the Report Service, which retrieves and aggregates the required records through the repository and data-access components.

The reporting function uses information from predictions, confirmed production decisions, POS simulation results, sales transactions, inventory movements, donations and waste records. These data sources allow the system to present measures such as predicted units, produced units, units sold, lost sales, estimated demand, leftovers, donations, waste, revenue, ingredient cost and gross profit. Calculations are performed by the backend to ensure that the mobile dashboard and exported reports use the same values and business rules.

Users may view reports using daily, weekly, monthly or custom date ranges. Results may also be filtered by bread category or presented as an overall bakery summary. Summary cards provide important totals, while tables and charts support comparison across dates and bread categories. For example, predicted quantities may be compared with actual or simulated units sold to identify forecasting differences and operational trends.

Because the proposed system uses a POS simulator, the origin of sales data must remain identifiable. Records generated by the simulator are labelled as simulated data and must not be presented as real bakery transactions. The corresponding report displays an appropriate simulated-data indicator, while the stored data\_origin value preserves this distinction for later analysis and model training.

Both the Bakery Manager and System Administrator may view operational and financial reports according to their authorised access. Report requests are validated before processing, and only the selected reporting period and permitted bakery data are returned. The generated results may be viewed through the mobile application and exported in CSV or PDF format for further analysis, documentation or presentation.

### **4.7.2 Operational and Financial Reports** {#4.7.2-operational-and-financial-reports}

The reporting module provides operational and financial reports using the daily results and related transaction records stored by the system. Operational reports support decisions concerning production, sales, inventory and leftovers, while financial reports summarise revenue, ingredient cost and gross profit. Table 4.25 describes the principal report contents.

*Table 4.25: Principal Operational and Financial Reports*

| Report | Main information | Principal data source | Purpose |
| :---- | :---- | :---- | :---- |
| Demand and Production Report | Predicted units, recommended production, confirmed quantity, actual produced quantity, units sold, lost sales and estimated demand | Daily Predictions, Production Decisions, Daily Production and Daily Results | Compares demand predictions with production and sales outcomes. |
| Sales Performance Report | Units sold, sales by bread category, time-slot sales and lost sales | Daily Results and Sales Transactions | Identifies sales patterns and possible unmet demand. |
| Leftover and Waste Report | Leftover quantity, leftover rate, donated quantity, wasted quantity and remaining unallocated leftovers | Daily Results, Donations and Waste Records | Evaluates surplus handling and bakery food-waste performance. |
| Financial Summary Report | Revenue, ingredient cost, gross profit and gross-profit margin | Daily Results, Sales Transactions and Inventory Logs | Summarises the financial outcome of bakery production and sales. |
| Inventory Report | Available quantity, inventory value, low-stock ingredients, expiring batches and inventory movements | Inventory, Inventory Batches and Inventory Logs | Supports ingredient replenishment and inventory monitoring. |
| Donation Report | Bread category, donation date, quantity, charity partner, status and confirmation information | Donations and Charity Partners | Provides traceability for products allocated to charity partners. |
| Trend Report | Predicted demand, estimated demand, units sold, lost sales, leftovers, revenue and donations across the selected period | Aggregated Daily Predictions and Daily Results | Identifies changes and recurring patterns over daily, weekly, monthly or custom periods. |

The principal derived values are calculated consistently by the backend using the following formulas:

* Estimated Demand \= Units Sold \+ Lost Sales 

* Leftovers \= Produced Units − Units Sold

* Leftover Rate \= (Leftovers​ / Produced Units) × 100%

* Revenue \= ∑(Quantity Sold × Unit Price)

* Gross Profit \= Revenue − Ingredient Cost

* Gross-Profit Margin \= (Gross Profit / Revenue​) × 100% 

Ingredient cost is calculated using the quantity and unit cost of the ingredient batches consumed through FIFO inventory deduction. The reported gross profit represents revenue minus direct ingredient cost; it is not treated as net profit because other expenses such as salaries, utilities and equipment costs are outside the project scope. Where a formula has a zero denominator, the corresponding percentage is displayed as “Not Applicable” to avoid a division-by-zero error.

Reports for multiple days aggregate the validated daily results within the selected date range. Bread-category filters restrict the calculations to the selected category, while the All filter produces an overall bakery summary. Sales-transaction records provide detailed time-slot information, whereas Daily Results provide the consolidated daily totals. These sources are not added together as separate totals, thereby preventing duplicated values.

When a report contains POS simulation results, the report displays a simulated-data label. This maintains the distinction between simulated estimates and real sales records while allowing the generated data to be analysed and used for approved model-training activities.

### **4.7.3 Report Export Design** {#4.7.3-report-export-design}

The system supports CSV and PDF export formats to allow authorised users to retain, analyse and present report information outside the mobile application. Exporting is initiated manually from the Reports and Analytics screen after the user selects the report period, bread-category filter and required file format.

The Flutter API Client sends the export request to the Report Controller. The Report Service validates the selected filters, retrieves the required records and calculates the report values. The Report Exporter then converts the results into the selected format and returns the generated file to the Android application. This design ensures that displayed and exported reports use the same data sources, calculations and business rules.

Table 4.26 compares the two supported export formats.

*Table 4.26: Export Format Design*

| Design aspect | CSV export | PDF export |
| ----- | ----- | ----- |
| Primary purpose | Further analysis using spreadsheet or data-analysis software | Formal presentation, printing and record keeping |
| Content | Structured rows and columns containing detailed and summary values | Report title, selected filters, summary indicators, charts, tables and explanatory labels |
| Visual formatting | Minimal formatting to preserve machine readability | Consistent BakeSmart headings, colours, page structure and table formatting |
| Date format | ISO-compatible date values | Human-readable dates based on the configured bakery timezone |
| Numeric format | Raw numeric values suitable for calculation | Formatted quantities, percentages and Malaysian Ringgit values |
| Chart support | Not included | Selected summary charts may be included |
| Simulated-data identification | data\_origin column and explanatory value | Visible “Simulated Data” label and explanatory note |

The exported PDF begins with the system name, report title, selected reporting period, bread-category filter and generation timestamp. Summary indicators are followed by relevant charts and detailed tables. A footer identifies the report-generation date and page number. When simulated POS data are included, a visible statement explains that the figures are simulated estimates and not real bakery transactions.

The CSV file uses a consistent header row and UTF-8 encoding. Each row represents a report record at the appropriate date and bread-category level. Dates use a consistent format, while monetary and percentage values are exported as numeric values so that further calculations can be performed. The data\_origin field distinguishes simulated records from any future actual sales records.

Generated files use a predictable and sanitised filename, such as:

* BakeSmart\_Weekly\_Report\_2026-07-27\_to\_2026-08-02.pdf

Only authenticated Bakery Managers and System Administrators may request report exports. The backend applies the same role and data-access checks used for on-screen reports, and confidential values such as passwords, authentication tokens, API keys and internal model files are never included. If report generation fails, the user receives an understandable error message and may retry without losing the selected report filters.

Export files are generated on demand and returned to the Android application for viewing, saving or sharing. Temporary server-side files are removed after delivery where temporary storage is required. This approach reduces unnecessary storage while providing users with portable and consistently formatted report outputs.

## **4.8 Security Design** {#4.8-security-design}

The security design applies defence-in-depth principles across the Flutter application, Express backend, FastAPI machine-learning service and Supabase platform. Security controls are applied at the presentation, API, business-service, data-access and database levels so that protection does not depend on a single component.

Supabase Authentication manages user credentials and authentication sessions. Passwords are handled by Supabase Authentication and are not stored in the application’s USER\_PROFILES table. After successful login, the Flutter application receives a signed JSON Web Token and attaches it to protected Express API requests using the Bearer authentication scheme. Sensitive session information is stored using secure device storage and is removed when the user logs out.

The Express authentication middleware validates the token signature, issuer, audience and expiry before accepting the request. The authenticated user identifier is then used to retrieve the user’s profile, account status and assigned role. Roles are obtained from the stored user profile and are never inferred from the user’s email address. Requests from inactive users or users without the required permission are rejected before the controller invokes the business service.

Table 4.27 summarises the principal role-based permissions.

*Table 4.27: Role-Based Access-Control Design*

| System function | Bakery Manager | System Administrator |
| :---- | :---- | :---- |
| Manage own profile | Permitted | Permitted |
| Generate demand predictions | Permitted | Not permitted |
| Review and confirm production decisions | Permitted | Not permitted |
| Run POS simulations | Permitted | Not permitted |
| Allocate leftovers to donation or waste | Permitted | Not permitted |
| View reports and dashboards | Permitted | Permitted |
| View and manage personal notifications | Permitted | Permitted |
| Manage ingredients, batches, categories and recipes | Not permitted | Permitted |
| Train, evaluate, activate and restore model versions | Not permitted | Permitted |
| Manage users and roles | Not permitted | Permitted |
| Modify approved system settings | Not permitted | Permitted |

Database access is protected using Supabase Row Level Security policies, foreign-key constraints, uniqueness constraints and validation checks. Direct Flutter access to permitted Supabase Realtime data is limited by the authenticated user and applicable policies. Server-side database credentials are stored only in backend environment variables and are never included in the Flutter application. If a privileged service credential is used by the backend, the Express business layer performs the required role and ownership checks before executing any database operation because privileged credentials may bypass Row Level Security.

Table 4.28 summarises the main security controls applied to the system.

*Table 4.28: Security Controls*

| Security area | Design control |
| :---- | :---- |
| Authentication | Supabase Authentication validates credentials and manages authenticated sessions. |
| API protection | Protected endpoints require a valid JWT, and unauthenticated or expired requests are rejected. |
| Authorisation | Express middleware and business services enforce role-based permissions before processing operations. |
| Database security | Row Level Security, keys, constraints and transactional operations protect stored records. |
| Input validation | Flutter provides immediate validation, while the backend independently validates all request data before processing. |
| Communication security | HTTPS protects API, authentication, database and external-service communication in transit. |
| Secret management | Database credentials, service-role keys, API keys and FCM credentials are stored in server environment variables and excluded from source code, reports and client responses. |
| Machine-learning security | The FastAPI service accepts validated requests from the Express backend, while model training, activation and restoration are restricted to the System Administrator. |
| Notification security | Device tokens are associated with authenticated users, notification preferences are checked and sensitive information is excluded from push-notification payloads. |
| Auditability | Important administrative and operational actions are recorded in system logs with the actor, event type, affected entity, outcome and timestamp. |

Client-side validation improves usability but is not treated as a security boundary. The Express backend validates required fields, data types, permitted values, numerical ranges and identifiers again before calling the business service. Database queries use the Supabase client or parameterised operations to reduce injection risks. Request-size limits and accepted content types are also applied to API endpoints.

Communication between the Flutter application and Express backend uses HTTPS with JSON and JWT. Communication from Express to Supabase and external services also uses HTTPS. The FastAPI machine-learning service is intended to be accessible through the Express backend rather than directly by mobile users. Requests to the machine-learning service are validated, and access to model artefacts and training operations is restricted.

Audit records are maintained for security-sensitive and important administrative actions, including user-role changes, model training, model activation, model restoration, setting updates and failed operations. Audit logs do not contain passwords, complete tokens, API keys or other secret values. Model versions and previous settings are retained where appropriate to support recovery from an incorrect administrative action.

Push notifications contain only the minimum information required to inform the user. Detailed operational information is retrieved after the authenticated user opens the application. FCM device tokens, delivery attempts and notification preferences are stored separately to support token deactivation and delivery tracking.

Error responses provide understandable messages without exposing stack traces, SQL statements, credentials or internal service details. Together, these controls protect authentication data, operational records, model-management functions and administrative settings while supporting the security requirements of the proposed system.

## **4.9 Algorithm Design**  {#4.9-algorithm-design}

### **4.9.1 Algorithm Design Overview** {#4.9.1-algorithm-design-overview}

The algorithm design defines how the system transforms historical, contextual and operational data into demand predictions, production recommendations, simulated sales results and leftover allocations. Machine-learning algorithms are handled by the Python/FastAPI service, while operational rules are controlled by the TypeScript business services. Table 4.29 summarises the principal algorithms.

*Table 4.29: Summary of Principal Algorithms*

| Algorithm | Main inputs | Main outputs | Responsible component |
| :---- | :---- | :---- | :---- |
| Demand Prediction | Historical units sold, temporal features, weather, holiday information and the active model | Next-day predicted units sold and confidence indicator | Python Prediction Engine |
| Cold-Start Prediction | Available recent records, configured category value and contextual factors | Heuristic demand estimate and cold-start status | Python Prediction Engine |
| Model Training and Evaluation | Validated historical records arranged chronologically | Candidate model, evaluation metrics, feature importance and model-version information | Python Model Training and Evaluation Engine |
| Production Recommendation | Stored prediction, recipes and available valid inventory | Feasible recommendation, maximum producible quantity and shortage information | TypeScript Recommendation Engine |
| FIFO Inventory Deduction | Confirmed production quantities, recipes and valid inventory batches | Updated batch quantities and inventory-movement records | TypeScript Inventory Service |
| POS Simulation | Confirmed production, stored prediction baseline, time-slot parameters and stochastic variations | Simulated units sold, lost sales, estimated demand, revenue and leftovers | TypeScript POS Simulation Service |
| Leftover Allocation | Available leftovers, selected action, quantity and charity partner where applicable | Donation or waste record and updated remaining leftovers | TypeScript Leftover Management Service |

Prediction generation, model retraining and POS simulation are manually initiated by authorised users. Required inputs and prerequisite records are validated before processing, while invalid or incomplete operations are rejected without storing partial results. The following subsections briefly describe the prediction and operational algorithms.

### **4.9.2 Demand Prediction and Cold-Start Algorithm** {#4.9.2-demand-prediction-and-cold-start-algorithm}

The demand-prediction algorithm estimates the next-day units expected to be sold for each active bread category. It uses historical units sold, lag and rolling-average features, temporal information, weather conditions and public-holiday information. When at least 30 valid daily records and an active model are available, the Random Forest model is used.

Let (T) be the number of trees and (pi) be the prediction generated by tree (i). The mean prediction is:

![][image37]

The stored prediction is converted into a non-negative whole quantity:

![][image38]

Model confidence is estimated from the agreement among the Random Forest trees. Let (σ) be the standard deviation of their predictions. The confidence indicator is calculated as:

![][image39]

A smaller difference among the tree predictions produces a higher confidence indicator. Predictions below the configured 75% threshold are labelled as Low Confidence. This indicator represents model agreement and is not interpreted as the probability that the prediction is correct.

When fewer than 30 distinct valid daily records are available for a bread category, the system applies the cold-start method. The base quantity (Bc​) is calculated from the average of the available valid records for category c. If no valid record is available, the configured base quantity for that category is used. The base quantity is then adjusted using the configured day-of-week, monsoon-season, weather and holiday factors:

![][image40]

where Dt, Mt, Wt and Ht​ represent the day-of-week, monsoon-season, weather and holiday adjustment factors for the target date t, respectively.

The result is stored with the prediction mode COLD\_START and is identified as a low-confidence heuristic estimate. It does not receive a numerical confidence value because the Random Forest tree-agreement confidence formula is not applicable when no trained model is used. Once at least 30 distinct validated daily records and a valid active model become available, subsequent manually initiated predictions use the Random Forest algorithm and receive a numerical confidence indicator.

### **4.9.3 Operational Algorithms** {#4.9.3-operational-algorithms}

The TypeScript business services apply several operational algorithms after a prediction has been generated. These algorithms ensure that the production recommendation is feasible, inventory is deducted correctly, POS results are calculated consistently and leftover allocations remain valid. Table 4.30 summarises their principal logic.

*Table 4.30: Operational Algorithm Summary*

| Algorithm | Principal processing logic | Result |
| :---- | :---- | :---- |
| Production recommendation | Account for confirmed but unprocessed production commitments and allocate the remaining temporary ingredient balance across unconfirmed categories in display order. Calculate each recommendation within that balance and verify the combined ingredient requirements of the production plan.  | Jointly feasible recommended quantities, maximum producible quantities and shortage information  |
| FIFO inventory deduction | Sort valid ingredient batches by received date, beginning with the oldest batch, and deduct the required quantity until the requirement is satisfied. | Updated batch quantities and inventory-movement records |
| POS simulation | Use the stored prediction as the demand baseline and apply configured time-slot and stochastic variations. Context already included in the prediction is not applied again as a demand multiplier. | Simulated transactions, units sold, lost sales, estimated demand, revenue and leftovers |
| Leftover allocation | Validate that each donation or waste quantity is positive and does not exceed the remaining unallocated leftovers. | Donation or waste record and updated remaining leftover quantity |

Production feasibility is evaluated across the complete production plan for the selected date rather than independently for each bread category. For every ingredient, the system multiplies each category’s planned production quantity by its recipe requirement and sums these quantities across the plan. The plan is feasible only when the combined requirement for every ingredient does not exceed the available valid inventory.

To generate recommendations, the system creates a temporary planning balance from inventory batches valid for the production date. It first accounts for ingredient requirements associated with existing confirmed but unprocessed production decisions for that date. If these commitments already exceed available inventory, the system reports the shortages and requires the plan or inventory to be corrected.

The remaining unconfirmed categories are processed in ascending display\_order. For each category, the maximum producible quantity is the largest whole-number quantity that can be produced without exceeding any ingredient’s remaining planning balance. The recommended quantity is limited to the lower of the predicted sales quantity and this maximum. Its ingredient requirements are then subtracted from the temporary balance before the next category is evaluated. This prevents the same available ingredients from being allocated repeatedly to different categories.

![][image41]

When the manager confirms or changes a quantity, the system recalculates the combined requirements using the proposed quantity and the other confirmed but unprocessed decisions for the same date. When an existing decision is revised, its previous quantity is replaced rather than counted again. Recommendations affected by a confirmed change are recalculated before further confirmation.

The temporary planning balance does not change stored inventory quantities or create inventory-movement records. Ingredient availability is revalidated and FIFO deduction is performed only when POS simulation begins. Decisions whose ingredients have already been deducted are not counted again as outstanding planning commitments. If simulation processing fails before the transaction is committed, all database changes made by that attempt are rolled back.

The main POS results are calculated as follows:

* Units Sold \= min(Simulated Demand, Produced Units)  
* Lost Sales \= max(0, Simulated Demand \- Produced Units)  
* Estimated Demand \= Units Sold \+ Lost Sales  
* Leftovers \= Produced Units \- Units Sold

For leftover management, the system enforces:

* Leftovers \= Donated \+ Wasted \+ Remaining Unallocated

Donation and waste actions require confirmation from the Bakery Manager and are not performed automatically.

## **4.10 Design for Non-Functional Requirements** {#4.10-design-for-non-functional-requirements}

The system architecture and detailed designs incorporate the non-functional requirements established in Chapter 3\. Table 4.31 summarises the principal design provisions without repeating the detailed architecture, security, database and user-interface discussions.

*Table 4.31: Design Provisions for Non-Functional Requirements*

| Quality attribute | Design provision | Related section |
| :---- | :---- | :---- |
| Performance | Indexed and paginated database queries limit displayed lists to 50 records. Contextual data are cached, report calculations are performed by backend services and machine-learning processing is separated into the FastAPI service. | Sections 4.2 and 4.5 |
| Security | Supabase Authentication, JWT validation, role-based access, Row Level Security, HTTPS and protected server-side configuration secure the system and its data. | Section 4.8 |
| Reliability | Transactional updates and rollback prevent partial FIFO deductions and operational records. The active model is retained when training or activation fails, while external-service failures provide retry or controlled fallback behaviour. | Sections 4.5 and 4.8 |
| Usability | Role-specific navigation, consistent visual components, clear validation messages and responsive Flutter layouts support the defined device sizes and user tasks. | Section 4.6 |
| Maintainability | The layered MVC architecture, modular services, repository interfaces, external-service adapters and configurable thresholds separate responsibilities and support future modification. | Sections 4.2–4.4 |
| Compatibility | The Flutter application targets Android 10 or later, while components exchange consistent JSON data through REST APIs. | Sections 4.2 and 4.4 |
| Data integrity | Primary keys, foreign keys, uniqueness rules, validation constraints, audit records and transactional processing protect stored data. | Section 4.5 |
| Prediction quality | Chronological holdout evaluation, Random Forest and Linear Regression comparison, MAE, RMSE, MAPE and R2, model versioning and origin-labelled evaluation support controlled model assessment. | Section 4.9 |

These provisions translate the measurable requirements from Chapter 3 into concrete architectural, data, interface and processing decisions. Their achievement will be verified through the corresponding testing activities during system implementation and evaluation.

## **4.11 Chapter Summary** {#4.11-chapter-summary}

This chapter presented the system design of the Smart Bakery Food Waste Reduction System based on the requirements established in Chapter 3\. A layered client–server architecture integrated with MVC was selected to separate the Flutter presentation layer, TypeScript application and business services, data access, Python/FastAPI machine-learning service, Supabase platform and external services. Modular design, Object-Oriented Design and component-based principles were applied to organise the system responsibilities.

The Four-Plus-One View Model described the system from logical, process, development, physical and scenario perspectives. The database design defined the entities, relationships, tables and integrity constraints required for authentication, prediction, inventory, production, simulation, leftovers, reporting, notifications and model management. The user-interface design presented role-specific navigation and the principal screens for the Bakery Manager and System Administrator.

The chapter also defined the operational and financial report design, security controls, principal prediction and operational algorithms, and design provisions for the non-functional requirements. Together, these designs provide a consistent and traceable blueprint for implementing, integrating and testing the proposed system.
